questions.title: Standardize response format in a shared project
questions.prompt:
An eight-person sales support team in a ChatGPT Business workspace uses a shared project for proposal reviews. The lead wants all responses in the project to follow "Three-line summary → Risk table → Next actions." Some members have personal custom instructions specifying other formats, such as long narrative responses. Requirements:

- (1) Continue using existing project chats and files.
- (2) **Do not affect personal use outside the project**.
- (3) Make the change **in one place**, without adding steps to every conversation.

What is the most appropriate approach?

options.text: Ask everyone to replace their personal format instructions with the team format.
Upload a response-format guide as a project file and ask members to request compliance with it at the start of every chat.
Specify the response format in project instructions under Project settings.
Create a workspace agent with the format in its instructions, share it with the team, and move future proposal reviews there.

questions.explanation:
Requirements (2) and (3) are decisive. ChatGPT project instructions apply only within the project and override global custom instructions. Changing one project setting therefore standardizes the format without changing personal settings. All four options can influence formatting, but only project instructions meet all three requirements.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: violates constraints)**: It works, but personal instructions affect conversations outside the project, violating (2), and eight separate changes violate (3).
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: It works but requires the same request in every conversation, violating (3). Behavioral rules such as formatting are more consistent in instructions than reference files.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: Project instructions apply to project chats and override global custom instructions, while preserving existing chats and files.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: overengineering)**: The format becomes consistent, but moving to an agent leaves the accumulated project context, violating (1). A new tool is excessive for one formatting change.

Also note: Shared projects always use project-only memory, so they do not reference members' outside memories or context.

**References**: [Projects in ChatGPT › Add project instructions](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/10169521-projects-in-chatgpt) · [Projects in ChatGPT › Collaboration in shared projects](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/10169521-projects-in-chatgpt)

questions.title: Sequence workspace-agent instruction creation and validation
questions.prompt:
An HR operations team in ChatGPT Enterprise is creating a workspace agent for benefits questions. The owner plans to draft instructions with the agent builder, test representative questions, and then make it available to colleagues. Order the steps according to OpenAI guidance and **their dependencies**.

- (1) In Preview, test representative inquiries, inspect outputs and tool use, and revise instructions based on results.
- (2) In Agents, select Create, describe the work goal, review the draft plan, and select Build this agent.
- (3) Select Create to create the agent, then invite teammates with Can chat access.
- (4) Refine instructions in the builder and add benefits policy files and required apps.

items.text: In Preview, test representative inquiries, inspect outputs and tool use, and revise instructions based on results.
In Agents, select Create, describe the work goal, review the draft plan, and select Build this agent.
Select Create to create the agent, then invite teammates with Can chat access.
Refine instructions in the builder and add benefits policy files and required apps.

questions.explanation:
The builder produces a draft plan from the goal description. Users refine it, test in Preview, and select Create when ready. Sharing is possible only after the agent has been created.

| Order | Step | Dependency | Basis |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | (2) Describe goals and review the draft | Starting point: the builder uses this description to create the draft. | Creating an agent with the agent builder |
| 2 | (4) Add instructions, files, and apps | A draft must exist before refinement in the builder. | Refinement step in the same section |
| 3 | (1) Test and revise in Preview | Instructions, files, and apps must be present to test them. | Preview an agent: test, review, adjust, then Create |
| 4 | (3) Create, then share with Can chat | An agent cannot be shared before it exists. | Access levels: create before sharing |

Also note: When editing an existing agent, select Update in the builder's upper-right corner to save changes. Version history can republish an earlier version. Can chat users can see configuration, including instructions and tools, so avoid placing sensitive content in instructions.

**References**: [ChatGPT Workspace Agents for Enterprise and Business › Creating an agent with the agent builder](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/20001143-chatgpt-workspace-agents-for-enterprise-and-business) · [ChatGPT Workspace Agents for Enterprise and Business › Preview an agent](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/20001143-chatgpt-workspace-agents-for-enterprise-and-business) · [ChatGPT Workspace Agents for Enterprise and Business › Access levels](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/20001143-chatgpt-workspace-agents-for-enterprise-and-business)

questions.title: Separate manuals from project instructions
questions.prompt: An HR team on Claude Team is improving a benefits guidance project. Its entire 120-page benefits manual and response rules are mixed together in project instructions. Most rules say "Do not...", and response format and tone vary. Choose **TWO** changes consistent with Anthropic's recommendations.

options.text: Move the manual into project knowledge and keep only response-behavior rules in instructions.
Repeat one nearly identical question-and-answer example many times in instructions to stabilize formatting.
Paste the manual and rules into the first message of each chat so that other chats in the project inherit that context.
Replace prohibitions with descriptions of the desired response, adding a one-line reason for each rule.
Blend examples naturally into instruction prose without tags separating them from instructions.

questions.explanation:
Claude's help describes project instructions as defining behavior and responses, and project knowledge as reference material used across the project's chats. Anthropic's prompting guidance recommends stating what to do rather than what not to do, explaining reasons, and using diverse examples enclosed in tags.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: It follows the distinction between behavioral instructions and reference knowledge.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: factual error)**: The guidance recommends three to five relevant, diverse examples to avoid learning unintended patterns.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: approach for another situation)**: Chats within a project do not share context, so text pasted in one does not carry into another. Material needed across chats belongs in knowledge; repeated pasting adds operational burden.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: Describing the desired behavior and its rationale helps Claude generalize rules.
- **{{option:E}} (Incorrect: factual error)**: Examples should be wrapped in `<example>` or `<examples>` tags to distinguish them from instructions.

**References**: [How can I create and manage projects? › Adding content to project knowledge](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/9519177) · [Prompting best practices › Add context to improve performance](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices) · [Prompting best practices › Use examples effectively](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices) · [Prompting best practices › Control the format of responses](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices)

questions.title: Overemphasized instructions cause excessive searches
questions.prompt: A finance lead on Claude Team tests financial inquiry instructions in a private project before rollout. The instructions say, "CRITICAL: Always search the internal wiki connector first for every question." Claude now searches even for simple proofreading requests, slowing responses. The lead wants to **retain wiki searches for policy questions** and make **the smallest change in one instruction location**. What is most appropriate?

options.text: Replace it with: "Search the wiki for questions about internal policies or procedures, because policies change frequently."
Keep the existing sentence and add an emphatic uppercase prohibition: "Never search for simple requests."
Disable the wiki connector and upload exported copies of frequently requested policy pages as project knowledge.
Keep the instructions and ask teammates to disable the wiki connector in the + menu for each simple conversation.

questions.explanation:
The decisive constraints are retaining wiki searches for policy questions and editing instructions in one place. Anthropic explains that newer Claude models are more sensitive to system prompts, so forceful wording such as "CRITICAL: You MUST...", originally intended to encourage tool use, can cause excessive calls. The recommended fix is plain conditional wording such as "Use this tool when..."; giving a reason improves generalization.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: It removes excessive emphasis, provides a condition and rationale, and changes only one sentence.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: factual error)**: More emphasis repeats the stated cause and conflicts with the recommendation to describe desired behavior rather than prohibitions.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: It reduces searches but prevents access to current wiki policies and creates ongoing copy-maintenance work.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: Per-conversation connector disabling is real, but requires repeated human action rather than one instruction change.

**References**: [Prompting best practices › Tool usage](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices) · [Prompting best practices › Add context to improve performance](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices) · [Use connectors to extend Claude's capabilities › Use connected services](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/11176164)

questions.title: Instruction layers and formatting: evaluate statements
questions.prompt:
A legal support lead at a company using Claude Team is designing a contract review environment. The Owner has already set organization instructions to "Write all responses in polite Korean." Mark each statement Yes only if **both its judgment and rationale** agree with Anthropic documentation; otherwise mark No.

1. If a member's personal instructions say "Answer in English and lead with the conclusion," organization instructions override personal instructions, so the entire personal instruction is ignored, including conclusion-first ordering.
2. The legal team's review checklist, about 2,000 characters, can be added to organization instructions by the Owner. Members cannot see organization instructions, so other teams' conversations are unaffected.
3. If bullets persist despite "Do not use Markdown" for plain-text Slack responses, replace it with "Write in smoothly flowing prose paragraphs." If necessary, reduce headings and bullets in the instruction text to match the desired output.
4. For three pasted contracts totaling about 40k tokens, guidance to wrap each contract in tags with source metadata and quote relevant clauses first, but place review questions before the contracts, follows the documentation.

items.text: If a member's personal instructions say "Answer in English and lead with the conclusion," organization instructions override personal instructions, so the entire personal instruction is ignored, including conclusion-first ordering.

The legal team's review checklist, about 2,000 characters, can be added to organization instructions by the Owner. Members cannot see organization instructions, so other teams' conversations are unaffected.

If bullets persist despite "Do not use Markdown" for plain-text Slack responses, replace it with "Write in smoothly flowing prose paragraphs." If necessary, reduce headings and bullets in the instruction text to match the desired output.

For three pasted contracts totaling about 40k tokens, guidance to wrap each contract in tags with source metadata and quote relevant clauses first, but place review questions before the contracts, follows the documentation.

questions.explanation:
This question tests how instruction placement (organization, project, or personal) and formatting affect results. Claude documentation says organization instructions apply to every organizational conversation and override conflicting personal instructions, while nonconflicting personal instructions remain active. Prompting guidance recommends describing what to do, matching prompt formatting to desired output, and placing long documents first and questions last. Each statement alters one condition.

- **1 (No)**: The language directly conflicts, so polite Korean wins. Conclusion-first ordering is not addressed by organization instructions and remains applicable. The claim that all personal instructions are ignored is wrong.
- **2 (No)**: Members cannot view organization instructions, but those instructions still enter every organizational conversation. Team-specific rules belong in that team's project instructions. Organization instructions should be short and contain behavior applicable equally to everyone, with a 3,000-character limit.
- **3 (Yes)**: The guide recommends "write in flowing prose paragraphs" instead of "do not use Markdown," and matching prompt formatting to the desired output if needed. Reducing Markdown in prompts can reduce it in outputs.
- **4 (No)**: Document tags, source metadata, and quoting relevant sections first are recommended. However, documents longer than roughly 20k tokens should appear first, with questions at the end. The guide says placing questions last can improve quality by up to 30%. Placing them first is incorrect.

Also note: Organization instructions are prompt-level guidance, so rare direct conflicts may produce variations. Test in a new conversation after saving.

**References**: [Set organization instructions › How organization and user instructions interact](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/14546867-set-organization-instructions) · [Prompting best practices › Control the format of responses](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices) · [Prompting best practices › Long context prompting](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices)

questions.title: When project knowledge approaches the context limit
questions.prompt: A legal support team on Claude Team has continuously added standard contracts, prior review notes, and clause commentary to a project. Most materials rarely change after upload. A notice says project knowledge is approaching the context-window limit. The team wants questions to reference multiple materials and seeks **the lowest operational burden**. What is most appropriate?

options.text: Split the project by document topic and have users select the appropriate project for each question.
Have an owner rewrite older files as summaries every week and replace originals to stay below the limit.
Ask IT to build a remote MCP server for the contract file server and connect it through a custom connector.
Paid plans automatically enable RAG mode near the limit, so continue adding materials to the current structure.

questions.explanation:
On paid Claude plans, approaching the project knowledge context limit automatically activates RAG mode and expands project capacity. Since these materials rarely change, static uploads remain suitable. Keeping the existing project avoids restructuring and minimizes operational burden.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: Knowledge is confined to each project, making cross-document questions harder and requiring users to choose projects repeatedly.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: Weekly manual work is introduced and original information is lost.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: overengineering)**: Unchanging material does not need live access, while server construction and operation add work.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: Team is a paid plan, so RAG activates automatically and expands capacity without extra work.

Also note: Chats within a project do not share context; material needed across conversations should be placed in knowledge.

**References**: [How can I create and manage projects? › Adding content to project knowledge](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/9519177)

questions.title: A team notebook requiring source-grounded answers and audio overviews
questions.prompt:
A quality team has created a notebook with 30 standard operating procedures as sources. It can open the notebook in Gemini Notebook or the notebook feature in Gemini Apps. Requirements:

- (1) Answers must use **only notebook sources**, without web search results.
- (2) Create an **Audio Overview** for new-hire training.
- (3) Share with six quality-team members, **without making it public outside the team**.

Which setup is most appropriate?

options.text: Chat with the notebook in Gemini Apps, add that chat to the sources panel as shared context, and share the notebook with teammates.
Chat in Gemini Notebook, create the Audio Overview in Studio, and share the notebook privately with the six teammates.
Chat in Gemini Apps, add "Answer only from sources" to notebook custom instructions, and have teammates do the same.
Chat in Gemini Notebook, create an Audio Overview, and use a public sharing link posted only in the team channel.

questions.explanation:
All three requirements matter. Gemini Notebook answers only from notebook sources, whereas Gemini Apps can use the same sources plus tools such as web search. Studio artifacts such as Audio Overviews can be created only in Gemini Notebook. Notebooks containing Gemini chats remain private and cannot be shared.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: violates constraints)**: Gemini Apps may mix in web search, violating (1); adding a Gemini chat prevents sharing, violating (3).
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: It provides source-grounded answers, Studio artifacts, and private team sharing.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: violates constraints)**: Custom instructions apply in both apps but do not change the Gemini app's ability to use other tools. Gemini Apps also cannot create the Audio Overview, violating (2).
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: Anyone with the link and a Google account can open a public notebook, regardless of where the link is posted, violating (3).

**References**: [Notebooks in Gemini Apps › Key differences between apps](https://support.google.com/gemininotebook/answer/17003757) · [Notebooks in Gemini Apps › Custom instructions](https://support.google.com/gemininotebook/answer/17003757) · [Create a notebook in Gemini Notebook › Share notebooks & artifacts publicly](https://support.google.com/gemininotebook/answer/16206563)

questions.title: Choosing source formats for a new-hire training notebook
questions.prompt:
A training operations team is creating a Gemini Notebook notebook. Candidate sources are Google Docs lessons, an internal wiki workflow page with text and diagrams, and an internal lecture video. Requirements:

- (1) Weekly lesson edits appear **without re-uploading**.
- (2) The lecture **cannot be made public**; it is currently private on YouTube.
- (3) The wiki’s **diagram content** must also support answers.

Select TWO actions that respect these requirements.

options.text: Export lessons as PDFs weekly, upload them, and delete previous PDF sources.
Import lessons from Google Drive so changes automatically synchronize into the notebook.
Make the YouTube lecture public, verify captions, and add its URL as a source.
Add only the wiki URL to import both text and diagrams.
Add wiki text through its URL and separately export and upload diagrams as image sources.

questions.explanation:
Requirements (1) and (3) are decisive; (2) eliminates a distractor. Drive sources automatically sync every few minutes and support manual sync. Web URLs import HTML text only, excluding images, embedded videos, and subpages. YouTube supports only public videos with captions. Images can be uploaded as separate source types.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Uploads work but are snapshots requiring weekly replacement, violating (1).
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: Automatic Drive sync keeps content current without re-uploading.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: A public video can be imported, but making it public violates (2).
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: URL sources import only text, omitting diagrams and failing (3).
- **{{option:E}} (Correct)**: URL text plus separate image sources satisfies (3).

Each source supports up to 500,000 words, with a 200MB limit for uploaded files. Some image formats may be recognized less accurately, so verify with representative questions after import.

**References**: [Add or discover new sources for your notebook › Understand source types & limitations](https://support.google.com/gemininotebook/answer/16215270)

questions.title: Provide team-wide access to a changing Drive folder
questions.prompt:
A 12-person procurement team in ChatGPT Business wants a shared tool for supplier contract questions. Evidence consists of 55 PDFs in one Google Drive folder, with several added or revised monthly. The administrator has enabled workspace agents and Google Drive. Requirements:

- (1) **Each member must ask questions directly**.
- (2) There must be **no monthly file reuploading**.
- (3) Manage instructions and source configuration **in one place**.

What is most appropriate?

options.text: Create a shared project, combine PDFs into at most 40 files, and replace changed contracts monthly.
Add the Drive folder link to the owner's private project and share individual chat links when colleagues need answers.
Add Google Drive as a workspace-agent tool, write its instructions, and share the agent with members using Can chat.
Have every member create a private project and add the same Drive link and instructions separately.

questions.explanation:
All three requirements are decisive. Adding app links as project sources is documented for private projects. Shared-project responses reference uploaded files and content shared directly into the project. Shared projects allow up to 40 files, which require reuploading when changed. Workspace agents can attach apps such as Google Drive, query original material at runtime, and be shared with multiple users.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: Combining files fits the limit and enables shared use, but monthly uploads remain, violating (2).
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: The source link works, but a single-chat recipient cannot access other project chats, files, or instructions; it does not let each member ask directly as required by (1).
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: Runtime Drive access avoids reuploads, one agent centralizes instructions and tools, and Can chat lets each member ask questions.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: Members can access current material, but instructions and configuration are scattered across 12 places, violating (3).

Also note: Google Drive added inside a project is not pre-synced or indexed, and ChatGPT may request confirmation before searching outside the project.

**References**: [Projects in ChatGPT › Add links from apps](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/10169521-projects-in-chatgpt) · [Projects in ChatGPT › Can ChatGPT’s responses in shared projects include private or internal data?](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/10169521-projects-in-chatgpt) · [Projects in ChatGPT › Share a single chat from your project](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/10169521-projects-in-chatgpt) · [ChatGPT Workspace Agents for Enterprise and Business › Add tools and apps](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/20001143-chatgpt-workspace-agents-for-enterprise-and-business)

questions.title: Use an oversized pricing spreadsheet as a notebook source
questions.prompt:
A sales planning team is creating a quotation notebook in Gemini Notebook. Its core source is a Google Sheets price list of about 250k tokens, edited directly in Sheets by several owners each week. Requirements:

- (1) **Every row** must be available as evidence.
- (2) Weekly changes must appear **without reuploading**.
- (3) Owners must continue editing in **their existing spreadsheet format**.

Which setup is most appropriate?

options.text: Split the price list into three separate Drive spreadsheet files of no more than 100k tokens each, edit those sheets, and import all three as sources.
Split the existing spreadsheet into three tabs of no more than 100k tokens each, then import that spreadsheet from Drive.
Export and upload the price list as a PDF each week, replacing the old PDF. The 500,000-word PDF limit accommodates every row.
Convert the price list to Google Docs and import it from Drive. Docs supports 500,000 words and automatic synchronization.

questions.explanation:
Requirements (1) and (2) are decisive, while (3) rules out {{option:D}}. Google Sheets sources are limited to 100k tokens, and multiple tabs in Google Docs or Sheets are combined into one source. Drive-imported sources sync automatically every few minutes. Separate spreadsheet files within the limit are therefore needed to retain all rows and automatic updates.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: Each file becomes a source within the Sheets limit; Drive sync reflects weekly edits, and owners still work in spreadsheets.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: factual error)**: Tabs combine into one 250k-token source, so (1) is not met.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: All rows fit, but the uploaded snapshot requires weekly replacement, violating (2).
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: The converted document is separate from the original spreadsheet, so spreadsheet edits do not propagate. Editing the document instead would violate (3).

**References**: [Add or discover new sources for your notebook › Understand source types & limitations](https://support.google.com/gemininotebook/answer/16215270)

questions.title: Connect an internal inventory server behind a firewall to sales-team Claude
questions.prompt:
A sales operations owner at a company using Claude Team is building a quotation assistant. Inventory changes frequently, so live connector access is needed instead of file uploads. IT has built a remote MCP server inside the company firewall. Sales PCs can access it over the corporate VPN. The owner lacks configuration rights and can only request changes from the Owner and IT. Requirements:

- (1) Sales primarily uses **claude.ai on the web and Cowork**.
- (2) Security policy prohibits **opening the server to the entire internet**.

Which connector approach and requests are most appropriate?

options.text: Use a remote custom connector; ask the Owner to add it to the organization and IT to allow Anthropic IP addresses through the firewall.
Use a remote custom connector and ask only the Owner to add it. Since sales PCs reach the server over VPN, leave the firewall unchanged.
Use local MCP and ask IT to register the server in Claude Desktop on every sales PC so the corporate network can be used.
Use a remote custom connector; ask IT to expose the server to the public internet, then ask the Owner to add it.

questions.explanation:
Requirements (1) and (2) matter; the PCs' VPN access is a distractor. The builder must decide which approach works in web and Cowork, and who must do what. Remote custom connectors connect from Anthropic's cloud rather than the user's device, across all Claude clients including claude.ai and Cowork. Only Owners can add custom connectors to Team or Enterprise organizations. A server behind a firewall requires IT to allow Anthropic IP addresses.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: Remote connectors support web and Cowork, and restricting access to Anthropic IPs satisfies (2). The tradeoff is an IT firewall change.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: factual error)**: Connections originate in Anthropic's cloud. Local PC connectivity does not help if the firewall blocks Anthropic.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: Local MCP in Claude Desktop can use the device's network to reach internal servers, but cannot serve claude.ai or Cowork, violating (1).
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: It connects but exposes the server to the entire internet, violating (2).

Also note: The Owner and IT perform actual URL and firewall configuration. Even after the Owner adds the connector, each sales member must connect to and enable it.

**References**: [Get started with custom connectors using remote MCP › Network requirements](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/11175166) · [Get started with custom connectors using remote MCP › Add a custom connector](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/11175166)

questions.title: Allow a read-only app for one role
questions.prompt:
A ChatGPT Enterprise workspace wants only the custom sales role to use SharePoint, solely for searching and referencing documents. Requirements:

- (1) **No other role** may use SharePoint.
- (2) It must be **read-only**, with no writes even after confirmation.
- (3) Future write actions must **not become enabled automatically**.

Choose **TWO** required settings.

options.text: Enable plugin use under the sales role's Plugins & connected data and use Select to choose only SharePoint.
Set SharePoint Permissions to Always ask so every action requires confirmation.
Enable only read actions under Actions, and set New actions to "Only enable new read actions."
Set New actions to "Disable new actions" to disable already-enabled write actions.
Enable SharePoint for the whole workspace and use instructions and announcements to tell only sales to use it.

questions.explanation:
All three requirements matter. OpenAI separates controls into three layers: Role access determines who can use an app, Actions determines what it can do, and Permissions determines when ChatGPT asks for confirmation. Role-level app control is available in Enterprise and Edu. Both role configuration ({{option:A}}) and action scope ({{option:C}}) are needed.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: Selecting the app in the custom role restricts access to sales.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: Always ask is real, but controls confirmation timing. Approved writes remain possible, violating (2).
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: Read-only current actions and automatic enablement of only future read actions meet (2) and (3).
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: factual error)**: New actions policy affects later additions, not actions already enabled.
- **{{option:E}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: Instructions and announcements are not access controls; other roles can still use the app, violating (1).

Also note: Microsoft apps such as SharePoint may need Microsoft Entra administrator consent. Consent alone does not enable actions; they must also be enabled under Actions.

**References**: [Admin controls, security, and compliance for plugins and apps › Role-based access control](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/11509118-admin-controls-security-and-compliance-in-connectors-enterprise-edu-and-business) · [Admin controls, security, and compliance for plugins and apps › App action controls](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/11509118-admin-controls-security-and-compliance-in-connectors-enterprise-edu-and-business)

questions.title: Control hard-to-reverse workspace-agent writes
questions.prompt:
A marketing team in ChatGPT Enterprise is building a workspace agent for weekly campaign summaries. It creates draft reports through Google Drive and deletes outdated drafts. Requirements:

- (1) Draft creation need not require human approval every time.
- (2) Deletion must **always receive confirmation before execution**, but remain possible after approval.
- (3) **Do not affect** other teams' regular ChatGPT conversation settings.

Assuming the app supports these controls, which configuration is most appropriate?

options.text: Ask the administrator to set the workspace Plugin permissions default to Always ask.
Set the agent's write approvals to Custom: Never ask for draft creation, and require confirmation for deletion.
Set all agent writes to Never ask, and add "Ask the user before deleting" to instructions.
Add "Do not request Drive document deletion" to Connector Action Constraints to block deletion requests.

questions.explanation:
Requirements (2) and (3) are decisive. Workspace-agent writes default to Always ask at runtime. Depending on the app, they can be set to Never ask or Custom approval for selected writes. Workspace Plugin permissions apply to ChatGPT conversations, while workspace agents follow agent-specific controls configured by their builder.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: confusing similar features)**: This real setting does not govern agents and affects workspace-wide conversations, violating (3).
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: Per-action Custom approvals separate automatic creation from confirmed deletion.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: An instruction sentence is not an execution-time confirmation control and cannot meet the "always" requirement.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: The constraint blocks deletion requests, including approved deletion, violating (2).

Also note: Connector Action Constraints restrict requests the agent can make, not data returned by connectors.

**References**: [ChatGPT Workspace Agents for Enterprise and Business › Manage write actions](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/20001143-chatgpt-workspace-agents-for-enterprise-and-business) · [ChatGPT Workspace Agents for Enterprise and Business › Connector Action Constraints](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/20001143-chatgpt-workspace-agents-for-enterprise-and-business) · [Admin controls, security, and compliance for plugins and apps › App action controls](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/11509118-admin-controls-security-and-compliance-in-connectors-enterprise-edu-and-business)

questions.title: Add approval before sending in a live workflow
questions.prompt:
A sales planning team uses a shared Live workflow in Gemini Enterprise Workflow Builder: "Receive quotation request → Draft quotation → Email customer." It now needs:

- (1) The owner must **review and approve the draft before sending**.
- (2) The **current Live version must continue running** during edits and testing.
- (3) Pending approvals must be visible in one place.

What is most appropriate?

options.text: Turn off the Live version, add an Approval step before sending, then turn it on again after checking.
Add Request info before sending in the last saved draft to ask the owner for confirmation, then Update.
Add Approval before sending in the last saved draft, test with Start simulation, save, then Update.
Leave the workflow unchanged and create a chat agent with instructions to get owner confirmation before sending.

questions.explanation:
Requirements (1) and (2) are decisive. Approval shows output to a human and permits the next step only after approval. Paused runs appear as "Needs Review" in Runs. Workflow Builder keeps drafts separate from Live, allowing testing without disrupting the current version.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: Approval is added, but turning off ends schedules and ongoing runs and stops the workflow for all recipients, violating (2).
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: confusing similar features)**: Request info asks for missing information; it is not an output approval procedure, failing (1).
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: Draft editing and Start simulation in Preview preserve Live execution; Approval and Needs Review satisfy (1) and (3).
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: Chat agents are generally nondeterministic; the documentation distinguishes workflows as appropriate for approval-dependent tasks. An instruction sentence does not guarantee (1).

Also note: The editor opens the last saved draft, so save before enabling a version. To save without activating, choose Save version only in the confirmation dialog.

questions.title: Separately controlling calendar lookup, modification, and deletion
questions.prompt:
An administration team on Claude Team wants to use the Google Calendar connector enabled by its Owner for meeting-room and event scheduling. The lead will request settings meeting these requirements:

- (1) Schedule **lookups run without confirmation**.
- (2) Creation and editing require **user confirmation every time**.
- (3) Claude **cannot delete** events.
- (4) Members **cannot loosen these settings** individually.

Which configuration is most appropriate?

options.text: Have the Owner set lookup to Always allow, creation and editing to Needs approval, and deletion to Blocked in Tool permissions.
Have each member allow lookup, require approval for creation and editing, and disable deletion in their own tool menu, with Owner guidance.
Have the Owner set lookup, creation, and editing to Needs approval and deletion to Blocked.
Have the Owner set lookup to Always allow and creation, editing, and deletion to Needs approval.

questions.explanation:
Requirements (3) and (4) are decisive. Team and Enterprise Owners can choose Always allow, Needs approval, or Blocked for permission categories or individual permissions in connector Tool permissions. These restrictions apply organization-wide and cannot be overridden individually.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: Three tool-level settings meet (1)–(3), and organization-wide enforcement meets (4).
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Personal tool disabling and approval settings exist, but users can change them anytime, violating (4).
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Deletion is blocked and centrally enforced, satisfying (3) and (4), but lookup also requires approval, violating (1).
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Lookup and editing approval are correct and centrally enforced, but Needs approval still permits deletion after approval, violating the prohibition in (3).

Claude restrictions narrow rather than expand source-system permissions. Members still need Calendar permission to modify events.

questions.title: Sharing a sensitive HR project
questions.prompt:
An HR team using Claude Enterprise creates a project containing evaluation criteria and compensation material. Requirements:

- (1) Only HR group members can access it.
- (2) The Contractor role cannot share any projects.
- (3) **Other regular teams’ project sharing remains unaffected**.

Which setup is most appropriate?

options.text: Privately share the project with the HR group and turn off Share projects in Organization settings for everyone, including Contractors.
Privately share the project with the HR group and merely exclude Contractors from that group.
Make the project public to Everyone at the organization and disable Share projects for Contractor in Roles.
Privately share the project with the HR group and disable Share projects for Contractor in Roles.

questions.explanation:
Requirements (2) and (3) are decisive. Claude projects can be public to the organization or private to invited people. Enterprise group sharing manages access by membership. Administrators can disable Share projects per role in the Capabilities tab of Roles; this role-based control is Enterprise-only.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It satisfies (1) and (2), but blocks new sharing organization-wide and converts public projects to private, violating (3).
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It meets (1) and (3), but group exclusion does not prevent Contractors sharing other projects, violating (2).
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It meets (2) and (3), but public visibility exposes the project organization-wide, violating HR-only access in (1).
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: Project-level private group sharing and role-level Contractor sharing restrictions meet the requirements without affecting other teams.

Group sharing is beta and requires “Share resources with this group” in group settings. Role changes can take up to 15 minutes to apply.

**References**: [Manage project visibility and sharing › Understand the two project visibility options](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/9519189-manage-project-visibility-and-sharing) · [Manage project visibility and sharing › Add and remove access to private projects](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/9519189-manage-project-visibility-and-sharing) · [Control project sharing for your organization › Set project sharing by role](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/9927533-control-project-sharing-for-your-organization) · [Control project sharing for your organization › Turn off public projects only](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/9927533-control-project-sharing-for-your-organization)

questions.title: Share a notebook containing confidential sources
questions.prompt:
An HR planning owner uses a Gemini Notebook containing 40 policy documents and one unfinalized compensation-reform draft. Fifteen colleagues now need to ask policy questions. Requirements:

- (1) They must ask questions and **open the supporting policy sources**.
- (2) The compensation draft must **not be exposed**.
- (3) They must **not create separate notebook copies**.
- (4) They must **not reshare the notebook**.

Choose **TWO** appropriate actions.

options.text: Share the existing notebook through Chat View to hide the source list and the draft.
Create a separate notebook with policy documents only, excluding the compensation draft, and share with teammates as Viewers.
Share as Editors for collaborative source management and tell colleagues not to open the draft.
Uncheck Allow copies in sharing settings.
Use a public link posted only in the internal team channel.

questions.explanation:
Requirements (2), (3), and (4) are decisive. Viewers have read-only access to shared sources and notes. Editors can add or delete sources and notes and reshare the notebook. Chat View hides sources and artifacts in the interface but does not remove underlying access. Copy creation is controlled through Allow copies in Share settings.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: confusing similar features)**: Chat View is not an access restriction; other routes may expose the hidden draft, so it cannot guarantee (2).
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: Excluding the draft removes access entirely. Viewers can open sources but cannot reshare, meeting (1), (2), and (4).
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: violates constraints)**: Editors can access the draft and reshare, violating (2) and (4).
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: Disabling Allow copies prevents recipients from duplicating the notebook, meeting (3).
- **{{option:E}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: Anyone with a public link and Google account can open it, regardless of where the link is posted.

Also note: Disabling Allow copies does not prevent recipients from manually transcribing visible content. Material that must not be exposed should never enter the shared notebook.

**References**: [Create a notebook in Gemini Notebook › Share notebooks privately](https://support.google.com/gemininotebook/answer/16206563) · [Create a notebook in Gemini Notebook › Create a private copy of a notebook](https://support.google.com/gemininotebook/answer/16206563) · [Create a notebook in Gemini Notebook › Share notebooks & artifacts publicly](https://support.google.com/gemininotebook/answer/16206563)

questions.title: Where to fix recurring format errors first
questions.prompt: An administration team tests an internal assistant with 20 representative questions. Seven answers are factually correct but inconsistently formatted, such as tables appearing unpredictably. A teammate suggests an external formatting-tool connector. The team wants **the smallest change** addressing the cause and a way to verify improvement. What is most appropriate?

options.text: Add a formatting connector, route every answer through it, and retest with 20 newly created questions.
Specify the desired format in instructions, add a few consistently structured examples, and rerun the same 20 questions.
Add a formatting example document to knowledge, leave instructions unchanged, and retest only the seven failures.
Upload the seven failed questions with model answers as knowledge, then rerun the same 20 questions.

questions.explanation:
If facts are correct and only formatting varies, the issue lies in instructions, not knowledge or tools. Anthropic describes examples as among the most reliable ways to establish format, tone, and structure. Google recommends consistent examples but warns that too many can cause overfitting. The same question set is needed for before-and-after comparison.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: overengineering)**: Adding a tool increases scope and operational burden without addressing instructions, while new questions undermine comparison.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: It fixes the cause in instructions and uses the same test set to measure improvement.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: confusing similar features)**: Behavioral rules belong in instructions. Retesting only failures can miss regressions elsewhere.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: approach for another situation)**: It reuses the test set but places test answers into knowledge, inflating results by fitting those questions while leaving general formatting problems and their instructional cause unchanged.

**References**: [Prompting best practices › Use examples effectively](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices) · [Prompt design strategies › Optimal number of examples](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/prompting-strategies) · [Prompt design strategies › Consistent formatting](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/prompting-strategies)

questions.title: Slack deployment and ticket-system connection
questions.prompt: Which setup meets [Requirement 1] and [Security requirements] with **the narrowest permissions**?
questions.context:
> **[Company overview]** Nuri Logistics is a midsize parcel and warehousing company using ChatGPT Enterprise. Administrators have enabled workspace agents and Slack integration.
>
> **[Existing environment]** Forty support agents ask each other questions in Slack #cs-help. The support FAQ is exported to PDF and uploaded as an agent file. Shipping tickets live in an internal system with a custom MCP built by IT, providing ticket lookup, creation, and deletion. An IT staff member owns the agent and performs all edits.
>
> **[Requirement 1]** When support agents mention the agent in #cs-help, it answers using the FAQ and, when needed, retrieves ticket status or creates tickets. The same agent is published in the ChatGPT channel, where quality staff receive detailed weekly support analysis by category.
>
> **[Requirement 2]** Run 30 representative questions before and after launch to check quality and fix each failure type at its source.
>
> **[Security requirements]** The agent must not delete tickets. Ticket-system access must be limited to this task's needs, preferably without using employee personal-account permissions.
>
> **[Note]** The lead suggests using Connector Action Constraints to prevent customer phone numbers from appearing in agent responses.

options.text: Create an Agent-owned account connection with a minimally privileged service account, and block ticket-deletion requests through Connector Action Constraints.
Use End-user account authentication so each support agent signs in separately, with writes set to Always ask.
Use the IT owner's personal account for an Agent-owned account connection, with Custom approval requiring confirmation for deletion.
Use a service account for an Agent-owned account connection and filter phone numbers from responses using Connector Action Constraints, as the lead suggested.

questions.explanation:
The decisive clues are mentioning the agent in #cs-help under [Requirement 1] and all [Security requirements]. Slack deployment requires shared authentication for every app connection. Agent-owned account is shared, so the person running it does not authenticate. OpenAI recommends service accounts where possible and access limited to necessary scope, warning that personal shared accounts let others initiate actions under that person's identity. Connector Action Constraints restrict what requests an agent can make and are suited to blocking deletion requests.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: It meets shared authentication, least-privilege service-account access, and deletion blocking.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: Slack agents require shared authentication for every app connection; this setup cannot be used in Slack.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: violates constraints)**: It works in Slack but uses personal permissions, contrary to security requirements. Custom approval permits deletion after confirmation, failing the prohibition.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: factual error)**: The lead's suggestion is a distractor. Connector Action Constraints do not filter returned data, and this setup does not block deletion.

Also note: While Slack deployment is enabled, only the owner can add or change apps and connectors.

Testing 30 representative questions under [Requirement 2] reveals three failure types:

- (1) Slack responses are accurate but too formal and long for chat. Weekly analysis reports in the ChatGPT channel are currently the right length.
- (2) Questions about last month's revised return policy receive old rules. The agent's FAQ PDF is the pre-revision version.
- (3) For "Tell me the ticket status," the agent guesses from the FAQ without checking tickets. The ticket-system MCP is missing from its tools.

Which combination fixes each cause with **minimal changes and no effect on other channels**?
questions.context:
> **[Company overview]** Nuri Logistics is a midsize parcel and warehousing company using ChatGPT Enterprise. Administrators have enabled workspace agents and Slack integration.
>
> **[Existing environment]** Forty support agents ask each other questions in Slack #cs-help. The support FAQ is exported to PDF and uploaded as an agent file. Shipping tickets live in an internal system with a custom MCP built by IT, providing ticket lookup, creation, and deletion. An IT staff member owns the agent and performs all edits.

> **[Requirement 1]** When support agents mention the agent in #cs-help, it answers using the FAQ and, when needed, retrieves ticket status or creates tickets. The same agent is published in the ChatGPT channel, where quality staff receive detailed weekly support analysis by category.

> **[Requirement 2]** Run 30 representative questions before and after launch to check quality and fix each failure type at its source.

>

options.text: (1) Add tone and length rules to base agent instructions; (2) replace the old FAQ; (3) add the ticket MCP and select Update.
(1) Add tone and length rules to Slack channel instructions; (2) add the revised FAQ but retain the old one for comparison; (3) add the ticket MCP and select Update.
(1) Add tone and length rules to Slack channel instructions; (2) replace the old FAQ; (3) add an instruction to retrieve ticket status from the ticket system and select Update.

- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: confusing similar features)**: Without the MCP tool, an instruction cannot retrieve tickets.

questions.title: Where to apply team response rules within a project
questions.prompt:
A 10-person HR team in a ChatGPT Enterprise workspace uses a shared project called “Benefits Inquiries.” The coordinator has Edit access but is not the owner. They want the team rule “Use polite language and organize answers in tables” to apply to every chat in the project. Some teammates have conflicting personal custom instructions, such as “Use a casual tone and prose.” Requirements:

- (1) The same rules apply to **every chat** in the project.
- (2) **Teammates have no additional tasks**.
- (3) The coordinator can change the rules **without the owner’s help**.

Which method is most appropriate?

options.text: Ask all teammates to remove tone and format preferences from personal custom instructions, then put the rules in project instructions.
Enter the rules in project instructions under Project settings and leave teammates’ personal instructions unchanged.
Put the rules in workspace agent instructions and have teammates use that agent instead of project chats.
Ask the owner to edit project instructions and send all future rule changes to the owner.

questions.explanation:
The decisive clues are requirements (2) and (3); conflicting personal preferences are a distractor. OpenAI help states that project instructions apply only inside their project and override global custom instructions. The Enterprise context table explains that chats within a project use project instructions rather than custom instructions. Members with Edit access can edit project instructions directly.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: The rule would apply, but custom instructions are not used inside the project anyway. Asking teammates to clean them up is unnecessary and violates (2).
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: One set of project instructions applies to every project chat without changing personal settings. Edit access lets the coordinator make changes directly.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: overengineering)**: It standardizes format elsewhere but leaves project-chat rules unchanged. Moving workspaces for one rule fails (1).
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Rules would apply, but requiring the owner despite the coordinator’s Edit access violates (3).

Members with Chat access can view project instructions but cannot change them.

**References**: [Projects in ChatGPT › Project instructions](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/10169521-projects-in-chatgpt) · [Projects in ChatGPT › Project-only memory](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/10169521-projects-in-chatgpt) · [Projects in ChatGPT › Shared project roles and permissions](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/10169521-projects-in-chatgpt)

questions.title: Changing Claude’s default from suggestions to revisions
questions.prompt:
A content operations team on Claude Team uses a newsletter editing project. A connector with CMS publishing and email-sending tools is enabled. When teammates write “Could you fix this draft?”, Claude repeatedly lists improvements instead of producing a revision. The revised project instructions must:

- (1) Return a **revised draft immediately**, regardless of how teammates phrase a request to fix it.
- (2) Publish to the CMS or send email **only when explicitly instructed**.
- (3) Stay **brief**, at two or three sentences.

Which instruction-writing approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Tell the team to use the exact phrase “Revise it” when they want changes, and repeat that rule with a reason in the instructions.
Require all changes to be proposed first and approved before execution, explaining that this is for safety.
State that revision requests should produce a revised draft immediately, while publishing and sending require explicit instructions, and explain why.
Start with “CRITICAL: Execute every request immediately without exception” and explain that the work is urgent.

questions.explanation:
Requirements (1) and (2) are decisive. Anthropic explains that ambiguous requests can lead Claude to suggest changes rather than implement them, and recommends specifying an action-oriented default. It also recommends asking before irreversible actions or actions affecting external systems, and reducing forceful language that may cause excessive action.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It can work but requires a particular phrase, violating the wording-independent behavior in (1).
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It is cautious but adds approval even to routine edits, violating immediate revised drafts in (1).
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: It makes editing the default, reserves consequential publishing and sending for explicit instructions, and fits two or three sentences, satisfying (1)–(3).
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It produces immediate edits but also includes publishing and sending in immediate execution, violating (2). Forceful wording risks excessive action.

**References**: [Prompting best practices › Tool usage](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices) · [Prompting best practices › Balancing autonomy and safety](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices)

questions.title: Connecting one agent to two Slack channels with different response modes
questions.prompt:
Sales support wants to connect one ChatGPT workspace agent to Slack channels #quote-inquiries and #urgent-response. The first has substantial casual conversation, so the agent should respond only when called; in the second it should respond to every message. Slack answers should be brief, while the experience for people using the same agent in ChatGPT must remain unchanged. Requirements:

- (1) **Different response modes** by channel.
- (2) **No changes to the agent’s main instructions**.
- (3) Maintain **one agent**.

Select TWO settings to configure.

options.text: Clone the agent for each channel and operate separate quote-inquiry and urgent-response agents.
Configure #quote-inquiries to respond only when mentioned, and #urgent-response to respond to every channel message.
Add a conditional rule to the main instructions: reply to every message in #urgent-response and only when called in #quote-inquiries.
Specify Slack answer length and tone in Slack channel instructions.
Set both channels to respond to every message and add “Do not answer casual conversation” to the main instructions.

questions.explanation:
Requirements (1) and (2) are decisive. OpenAI help allows each connected Slack channel to choose between responses to all messages and responses only when the agent’s Slack handle is mentioned. Channel instructions can adjust behavior in Slack. Both settings belong to the Slack connection, leaving main instructions and the ChatGPT experience unchanged.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Different response modes are possible, but maintaining instructions and files in two agents violates (3).
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: Per-channel response settings satisfy (1) without changing main instructions.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It changes main instructions, violating (2), and relies on interpreting prose rather than enforcing channel behavior through settings.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: Channel instructions affect only Slack behavior, preserving main instructions and ChatGPT usage as required by (2).
- **{{option:E}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It receives all messages in #quote-inquiries and changes main instructions, violating (1) and (2).

While Slack deployment is enabled, only the owner can add or change apps and connectors.

questions.title: Matching requirements to instruction components
questions.prompt: An AI champion drafting a customer-inquiry assistant’s instructions is mapping five requirements to instruction components. Match each requirement to the most appropriate component. One component is unused.

options.text: Role definition
Output format specification
Examples of ideal responses
Actions requiring confirmation and their conditions
Reasons and background for rules
Connector to a source system

items.text: Start by explaining whom the assistant serves and what work it handles.
Require every answer to have three sections: conclusion, evidence, and next action.
Include three actual support sentences to demonstrate the desired tone.
Require staff confirmation before irreversible actions such as finalizing refunds or sending email.
Explain that the rule against asserting an amount definitively exists to prevent customer disputes.

questions.explanation:
This question tests how to map instruction content—role and task, answer structure, examples, confirmation conditions for risky actions, and reasons for rules—to appropriate design components. Anthropic notes that even a one-sentence role helps; desired formats should be expressed as what to do rather than what to avoid. It recommends 3–5 examples, asking before irreversible actions, and adding context to rules to improve performance.

| Item | Match | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | {{option:a}}: Role definition | Specifying the audience and task defines the role in one or two sentences. |
| 2 | {{option:b}}: Output format specification | Conclusion, evidence, and next action define the answer’s structure. |
| 3 | {{option:c}}: Examples | A few actual responses communicate tone more precisely than a description. |
| 4 | {{option:d}}: Confirmation actions and conditions | Specify that a person must confirm before irreversible actions execute. |
| 5 | {{option:e}}: Reasons and background | Explaining why a rule exists helps the model generalize its intent to similar situations. |
| — | {{option:f}}: Unused | A connector links an external system and is unrelated to these five requirements for instruction text. |

questions.title: Keeping procedures and templates consistent for 15 people
questions.prompt:
A 15-person quotation team on Claude Team wants everyone to use the same version of its quotation procedure and 12-page quotation template file. Both are revised quarterly. Requirements:

- (1) **No dependence** on centralized deployment by an Owner.
- (2) The assistant references the **actual 12-page template file**.
- (3) Revisions require changes in **only one place**.

Which setup is most appropriate?

options.text: Package the procedure and template as a skill ZIP, have all 15 teammates upload it individually to claude.ai, and distribute a new file for each revision.
Ask the Owner to put the procedure and template content into organization instructions and update those instructions for every revision.
Transcribe the template’s fields into project instructions and share the project with teammates.

questions.explanation:

Anthropic documentation states that custom skills in claude.ai are individual: teammates must upload them themselves, and they cannot be shared organization-wide or centrally managed by administrators. Claude projects, however, can be shared with members on Team and Enterprise, and those members use the same knowledge and instructions.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: The skill works, but all 15 people must re-upload each revision, violating (3).
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Everyone gets the same content, but it depends on the Owner’s work, violating (1).
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: A shared project provides one management location, but transcribed fields are not the actual template file, violating (2).

questions.title: Resolving conflicting instruction rules
questions.prompt:
A returns assistant’s instructions say both “Always answer in no more than three sentences” and “Cite the terms-and-conditions clause numbers in every response.” Testing 12 representative questions shows inconsistent answer length in five cases because citing all applicable clauses exceeds three sentences. The revision must:

- (1) **Retain both requirements**.
- (2) Change only **one or two sentences**.
- (3) Produce **consistent results** when retested on the same 12 questions.

Which revision is most appropriate?

options.text: Delete the three-sentence rule, keep only the clause-number requirement, and explain why.
State that clause citations take priority, collect the numbers at the end, and limit the body to three sentences, explaining why.
Prefix each rule with “Extremely important” and say both must be followed, explaining why.
Add five ideal answers for the five problematic question types and explain why.

questions.explanation:
Requirements (1) and (2) are decisive. The inconsistency arises because instructions do not specify which rule takes priority when they conflict. Anthropic recommends clear, direct requests and explains that reasons help Claude generalize rules. Defining priority and the exception with a reason resolves the conflict with the smallest change.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It eliminates the conflict by removing a requirement, violating (1).
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: It retains both requirements and specifies priority and citation placement in one sentence, supporting consistent retesting.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It adds little length but still leaves priority undefined. Forceful wording can cause excessive behavior and does not ensure (3).
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Examples are useful, but five new examples exceed the one- or two-sentence change allowed by (2).

**References**: [Prompting best practices › Be clear and direct](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices) · [Prompting best practices › Add context to improve performance](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices)

questions.title: Fixing a summarization project that adds unrequested sections
questions.prompt:
A planning team on Claude Team uses a meeting-minutes summarization project. Outputs repeatedly add unrequested “Recommended Actions” and “Risk Analysis” sections. The team wants only “Summary,” “Decisions,” and “Owners.” The instructions must:

- (1) **Always** include those three sections.
- (2) Prevent unnecessary sections **without manual cleanup**.
- (3) Fit within **one paragraph**.
- (4) Follow Anthropic’s recommended approach.

Select TWO appropriate revisions.

options.text: State that the output consists of Summary, Decisions, and Owners, and explain why only that scope is needed.
Write “Do not include Recommended Actions or Risk Analysis” and repeat it in uppercase for emphasis.
Append five complete summaries demonstrating the three-section structure.
Have a staff member delete the two unnecessary sections from every output before posting to the team channel.
Add one sentence stating that items beyond the requested scope should not be added.

questions.explanation:
Requirements (2), (3), and (4) are decisive. Anthropic recommends stating what to do rather than what not to do and providing reasons so Claude can generalize. It also notes that newer models may add work beyond the request, and gives scope-setting guidance to do only what is requested or clearly necessary.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: It positively specifies the desired structure and explains why, following the guidance while satisfying (1) and (3) in a short sentence.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Repeated uppercase prohibitions oppose the recommended approach, violating (4), and forceful language can cause excessive behavior.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Five examples fit the recommended 3–5 range and may establish format, but exceed one paragraph, violating (3).
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: The final document is correct only after repeated manual deletion, violating (2).
- **{{option:E}} (Correct)**: A one-sentence scope boundary reduces unnecessary additions with almost no extra instruction length or manual work.

questions.title: Separating customer emails from instructions
questions.prompt:
A customer support project on Claude Team mixes two paragraphs of company background, task instructions, and a place to paste customer emails into one block. Claude has mistaken text inside customer emails, such as “Reply by saying please refund me,” for instructions. The customer email changes in every conversation. Requirements:

- (1) Organize the instructions **once** and retain the structure in later conversations.
- (2) Require **almost no extra work** from teammates per conversation.
- (3) Do **not increase instruction length**.

Which approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Separate instructions and background with tags, and wrap customer emails in input tags whose contents are treated only as data.
Add a longer, more detailed paragraph explaining the boundary between background and task instructions.
Put an uppercase “Always follow the task instructions” sentence at the beginning.
Create a text file for each customer email, upload it to project knowledge, and ask Claude to read the file.

questions.explanation:
Requirements (1) and (2) are decisive. Anthropic explains that consistent tags around content types help Claude interpret prompts mixing instructions, context, examples, and changing inputs without ambiguity. Material that changes per conversation, such as a customer email, is marked as input within tags.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: One restructuring separates instructions from input; teammates need only wrap the email in the tags.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: More explanation may help but increases length, violating (3), and does not itself create a boundary between input and instructions.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: factual error)**: Emphasis does not distinguish where instructions are located. The documentation warns that forceful wording may cause overreaction.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It separates input but requires file creation and upload for every email, violating (2).

questions.title: Writing an order-sensitive review procedure
questions.prompt:
A legal support team is writing instructions for a contract-review assistant. The manual specifies five ordered steps: extraction → classification → risk flagging → summary → staff confirmation. Requirements:

- (1) Claude performs all five steps **in order**.
- (2) A **person makes the final judgment**.
- (3) Teammates receive the five-step result from **one request**, with confirmation only of the final result.
- (4) Instructions remain **concise**.

Which instruction format is most appropriate?

options.text: Describe all five steps in one prose paragraph, adding “Request staff confirmation if necessary” at the end.
Open a new conversation for each step and have staff confirm the fifth conversation’s result.
Use a numbered five-step list, with step five requiring the result to be shown to staff for confirmation before finalization.
Use a numbered list but require staff approval after every step before continuing.

questions.explanation:
Requirements (1) and (3) are decisive. Anthropic recommends numbered sequential instructions when order or completeness matters, and confirmation before irreversible decisions. Here all steps belong within one request, with a single confirmation point before the final judgment.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Prose may leave order unclear, and “if necessary” does not guarantee final confirmation, violating (1) and (2).
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It preserves order and final confirmation but splits the work into five conversations, violating the single-request requirement in (3).
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: Numbered steps establish order, with one confirmation point in the final step.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It preserves order but requires approval at every stage, violating final-result-only confirmation in (3) and creating approval fatigue.

**References**: [Prompting best practices › Be clear and direct](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices) · [Prompting best practices › Balancing autonomy and safety](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices)

questions.title: Writing confirmation criteria for irreversible actions
questions.prompt:
A purchasing team is defining human-confirmation rules for a purchase-request assistant. Current tools support lookup, draft saving, deletion, external sending, and publishing, and more may be added. Requirements:

- (1) Avoid **approval fatigue**.
- (2) Confirm **every** permanent or externally consequential action, including deletion, external sending, and publishing.
- (3) Keep the rule **short**.
- (4) Apply the same rule to **future tools**.

Which instruction is most appropriate?

options.text: “Ask the user for confirmation before every action, including lookup and draft saving.”
“Use sufficient caution before performing irreversible actions such as deletion or external sending.”
“Before using deletion, external-sending, or publishing tools, show the user the details and obtain confirmation.”
“Perform easily reversible actions directly; for irreversible or externally consequential actions, summarize the action and obtain confirmation before execution.”

questions.explanation:
Requirements (2) and (4) are decisive. Anthropic recommends allowing locally reversible actions while asking before actions that are difficult to undo, affect shared systems, or may be destructive. The criterion is reversibility and scope of impact, rather than tool names.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It satisfies (2) but requires approval even for lookups, violating (1).
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It is short, but “use caution” does not require confirmation and cannot ensure complete coverage under (2).
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It covers current tools but a named list excludes future tools, violating (4).
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: Categorizing by reversibility and impact allows immediate lookups, requires confirmation for permanent effects, and applies to new tools.

**References**: [Prompting best practices › Balancing autonomy and safety](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices)

questions.title: Turning an operating manual into assistant instructions
questions.prompt: A team is converting a 30-page PDF operating manual into assistant instructions. Arrange the steps according to their **dependencies**.

items.text: Test the assistant on 20 representative questions and collect answers that fail the criteria.
Extract always-applicable rules and exceptions from the manual.
Locate the source of each failure type, revise the instructions, and retest with the same questions.
Organize the extracted rules’ priorities and output format into a draft instruction set.

questions.explanation:
A draft organizes rules extracted from the manual; testing requires a draft; and revision requires failures revealed by testing. Anthropic recommends clear, direct instructions and reasons. OpenAI help recommends testing an agent in Preview and adjusting it based on results.

| Order | Step | Dependency | Supporting guidance |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | (2) Extract rules and exceptions | Start by determining what to transfer from the manual. | Be clear and direct: specify desired behavior. |
| 2 | (4) Organize priorities and format, then draft | Rules must exist before their priorities can be defined. | Add context: explain reasons and ordering. |
| 3 | (1) Test representative questions | Testing requires a draft. | Preview an agent: test and adjust. |
| 4 | (3) Revise by failure type and retest | Failed answers identify what needs changing. | Preview an agent: adjust based on results. |

Retest with the same question set used before the revision so results can be compared.

questions.title: How a sales manager should start a first workflow

- (2) Start by **describing the work in natural language** to obtain a draft.

- (4) Test behavior before publishing.

Which starting method is most appropriate?

Send requirements to an administrator and ask them to create the workflow in the admin console.
Describe the work in natural language, refine the generated workflow in the visual editor, and test it in simulation.
Start with a blank visual editor, place each step manually, and test the completed workflow in simulation.

questions.explanation:
Requirements (2) and (3) are decisive. Google documentation states that Workflow Builder lets employees and non-administrators build agents and workflows using natural-language prompts or a visual editor, then preview and simulate them in an integrated testing environment.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Code-based methods exist, but this is not a nondeveloper building it personally, violating (1) and (3).
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It may produce a working result, but the employee does not build it directly, violating (3).
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: Natural-language drafting, visual refinement, and simulation satisfy all four requirements.
