questions.title: Restoring a live agent after an instruction regression
questions.prompt:
A coordinator edited a live benefits agent’s instructions in a ChatGPT Enterprise workspace. It now answers some previously successful representative questions incorrectly. Forty teammates continue using it. Recovery must:

- (1) Give teammates **correct answers during recovery**.
- (2) **Identify** the change that caused the regression.
- (3) Preserve the **existing sharing configuration** and teammates.

Which approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Republish the previous version from Version history, test the revised instructions in Preview, and then select Update.
Create a new agent with the previous instructions and tell teammates to switch to it.
Add an “In this case, answer this way” exception for every failed question and select Update.
Duplicate the agent, fix the copy, and reshare the copy with teammates after testing.

questions.explanation:
Requirements (1) and (3) are decisive. OpenAI help explains that previous versions can be reviewed and republished, while access is managed separately through Share. It also recommends testing sample prompts in Preview before applying changes.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: Republishing restores correct answers immediately. The same agent retains its sharing configuration, while representative Preview tests isolate the problematic change.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It restores correct responses but moves teammates to a new agent, violating (3).
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Accumulated exceptions may fix individual questions while leaving the underlying change unidentified, violating (2).
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: The copy can be edited safely, but the original continues serving incorrect answers during recovery, violating (1), and sharing must be rebuilt.

questions.title: A Workflow Builder agent cannot read the internal CRM

A nondeveloper sales employee in Gemini Enterprise built a “Customer Visit Record Organizer” in Workflow Builder. They already have access to Workflow Builder, but the agent cannot read internal CRM data. The troubleshooting actions must:

- (1) Be checks the **builder can perform without coding**.
- (2) Stay **within administrator-defined controls**.

Select TWO appropriate actions.

Ask the administrator whether the CRM connector is provisioned and request it if missing.
If the connector exists, check whether administrator-approved permissions include CRM reading and request an adjustment.
Switch to a larger model to see whether the access step starts working.
Ask developers to build a replacement ADK agent that calls the CRM directly.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Embedding personal credentials falls outside administrator-defined controls, violating (2), and is inappropriate for security.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: Connector provisioning is the first check, and the builder can investigate and request it without code.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: An existing connector still cannot read without appropriate permission. This check meets both requirements.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: approach for a different issue)**: Model capability is unrelated to access permissions and does not change the cause.
- **{{option:E}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: A code-based replacement is not something the nondeveloper builder can do directly, violating (1).

questions.title: Using a 700MB catalog and weekly inventory sheet as agent sources
questions.prompt:
A ChatGPT Enterprise sales team is creating a workspace agent. Its sources are a product catalog PDF of about 700MB, revised annually, and a weekly updated inventory sheet in Google Drive. Requirements:

- (1) Agent files stay within the **512MB per-file limit**.
- (2) Only the **approved catalog PDF** is used; interim revisions must not appear.
- (3) Inventory values stay current **without re-uploading**.

Which setup is most appropriate?

Split the catalog into files no larger than 512MB and upload them; export and replace the inventory file in Files every week.
Keep both the catalog PDF and inventory sheet in Drive and connect the Google Drive app as a lookup tool.
Split the catalog into files no larger than 512MB in Files and read inventory through the Drive app tool.

Apps are tools connected through + Add tool; a connected sheet provides access to the original rather than an uploaded copy.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Inventory handling is appropriate, but 700MB exceeds the 512MB limit in (1).
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Catalog handling is appropriate, but weekly inventory uploads violate (3).
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It avoids uploads and file limits, but reading an editable catalog source violates the approved-PDF-only requirement in (2).
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: The rarely changed approved catalog is fixed as split uploaded copies, while frequently changing inventory is read through the app, satisfying all three requirements.

questions.title: Restricting search to legally approved documents through administrator sync
questions.prompt:
A ChatGPT Enterprise administrator in a workspace with a supported Google Drive connection wants all employees to search only legally approved documents. They are in three folders on a shared drive. Personal-drive documents and image files must not be searchable. Requirements:

- (1) Everyone searches the **same approved document set**.
- (2) Search is limited to **designated folders**, excluding images.
- (3) Employees perform **no individual setup**.

Select TWO settings.

Restrict the Google Drive app’s direct-action policy to read-only operations.
Set Google Drive app permissions to Always ask before every operation.
Use role-based access control to allow only the legal role to access Google Drive.
Exclude image file types from indexing in the same sync source.

Requirement (2) is decisive. OpenAI help states that supported workspaces can restrict administrator-managed Google Drive sources to specific shared drives or folders and exclude file types from indexing. Sync controls and live app-action controls are separate; direct-action restrictions may not limit content retrieved from a synchronized index.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: Folder-scoped sync excludes personal-drive documents, satisfies (1) and (2), and requires no employee setup.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: confusion between controls)**: Direct-action restrictions govern operations, not the synchronized index’s scope.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: confusion between controls)**: This determines when approval is requested, not what is indexed.

questions.title: Sharing quarterly policy PDFs with 20 teammates
questions.prompt:
An HR team on Claude Team is building an assistant for 20 teammates to query eight policy PDFs revised quarterly. The coordinator first tried querying the policy folder through the Google Drive connector. Requirements:

- (1) All 20 teammates ask questions **individually and directly**.
- (2) Instructions and materials are managed in **one place**.
- (3) Minimize the coordinator’s **revision work**.

Which setup is most appropriate?

options.text: Share the coordinator’s chat querying Drive-connected policies with all 20 teammates.
Share a project containing the eight uploaded PDFs with the team and replace them with revised files quarterly.
Have all 20 teammates create individual projects and connect the policy folder through Drive.
Have teammates upload the eight PDFs into personal projects and ask all 20 to replace them whenever revised.

questions.explanation:
Requirements (1) and (2) are decisive. Anthropic states that Team and Enterprise chats containing synced connector content cannot be shared, and each member must authenticate connectors individually. Projects can be shared on these plans so members use common knowledge and instructions. Since revisions occur only quarterly, replacing static uploads is sufficient.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: The chat contains synced connector content and cannot be shared. Even if shareable, it would not let teammates directly ask their own questions, failing (1).
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: One shared project holds instructions and PDFs, everyone can ask questions, and updates require one quarterly file replacement.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Everyone may access current material, but separate projects and connector authentication violate one-place management in (2).
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: All 20 must replace files and the coordinator must request and verify it, violating minimal revision work in (3).

questions.title: An edited recording is not reflected in notebook answers
questions.prompt:
A training team added a directly uploaded lecture recording and a YouTube training-video link to a Gemini Notebook notebook. After re-editing the recording into a new file, answers still reflect the old recording. Requirements:

- (1) Answers reflect the **edited content**.
- (2) **Old recording content** no longer appears.
- (3) Other sources and notebook settings stay unchanged.

Which action is most appropriate?

options.text: Wait a few minutes for automatic synchronization, as with Drive-imported sources.
Select “Click to sync with Google Drive” in the source list to force synchronization.
Import the edited file as a new source and delete the old recording source.
Add the edited file as a new source and retain the old recording source.

questions.explanation:
Requirements (1) and (2) are decisive. Google help explains that audio is transcribed once at import and saved as a new source. Files imported from Drive are the sources that automatically sync every few minutes. Changing an original directly uploaded recording therefore does not update its existing source.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: factual error)**: Automatic sync applies to Drive imports, not directly uploaded recordings, so waiting changes nothing.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: approach for a different situation)**: The manual sync button applies to Drive sources and does not update directly uploaded audio.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: Importing the new file supplies edited content; deleting the old source removes obsolete content, satisfying (1) and (2).
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: New content becomes available, but the old active source may still appear in answers, violating (2).

questions.title: Review comments in Docs do not appear in notebook answers
questions.prompt:
A legal team has 20 contracts in Google Docs, with review feedback in comments and footnotes. After importing the contracts from Drive into Gemini Notebook, answers contain none of that feedback. Requirements:

- (2) Include review feedback in **notebook answers**.
- (3) Preserve Drive synchronization so feedback updates need **no source re-upload**.

Disable and re-enable the 20 sources to reload their content.
Create contract copies, move comment and footnote feedback into their body text, and import the copies as Drive sources.
Create a separate Google Docs document collecting review feedback and add it as a Drive source.
Add “Also refer to the contracts’ comments and footnotes” to notebook custom instructions.

- (3) The manager configures it **personally without code**.

Which setup is most appropriate?

options.text: Use manual starts for both and invoke the workflow with @ and its name in chat when needed.
Use a Gmail app event trigger for incoming requests and a schedule trigger for the daily morning run.
Use schedules for both and process all received requests together each morning.
Ask developers to write an ADK email watcher and daily runner.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Manual starts require a person and violate both (1) and (2).
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: Events start on receipt and schedules start each morning, without code.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Requests wait until morning, violating immediate start on receipt in (1).
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: overengineering)**: It can work but needs code, violating (3), and uses development resources for built-in editor trigger functionality.

questions.title: One member still cannot read a folder after organization permissions are enabled

A is connected to the connector, but opening the documents directly in Drive also shows access denied. Which action is most appropriate?

Change read-tool permissions from Always allow to Needs approval.
Have the Owner remove and re-add the organization’s Drive connector.
Have A disconnect and reconnect the Drive connector using the same account.

Claude help explains that Owner tool permissions can narrow access but cannot grant more access than the source system allows. Always allow does not make documents readable without Drive permission. Other members can read because they have their own permissions. Direct access also fails, identifying source permissions as the cause.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: Granting A source-folder access enables reading through A’s connection.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: confusion between controls)**: Approval settings govern confirmation during execution; they do not grant read access.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: overengineering)**: Removing and re-adding the organizational connector requires everyone to reconnect while leaving A’s missing permission unchanged.

questions.title: Personal-use rules for a team overusing Always allow
questions.prompt:
Ten sales teammates each use Claude Pro and personally added a remote MCP connector with lookup, editing, and deletion tools for a partner system. Most have selected Always allow to avoid dialogs. The team lead wants a shared personal-use standard that:

- (1) Does **not interrupt routine lookups** with approvals.
- (2) Prevents erroneous editing or deletion from **executing immediately**.
- (3) Creates **little setup burden**.

Which standard is most appropriate?

options.text: Set every tool that shows approval dialogs to Always allow so conversations are uninterrupted.
Require approval for every call to every tool and carefully read each dialog.
Do not use remote MCP connectors for work; handle all material through file uploads.
Enable only necessary tools from trusted servers; always allow lookups but disable editing and deletion or approve them individually.

questions.explanation:
Requirements (1) and (2) are decisive. Claude help recommends Always allow only for trusted servers and tools, disabling tools unnecessary for the conversation, and understanding write and delete behavior before permitting it. Separating reads from writes reduces routine friction while reserving confirmation for irreversible actions.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It is convenient but lets erroneous edits and deletions execute immediately, violating (2).
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It is cautious but interrupts every lookup, violating (1), and approval fatigue may encourage careless clicks.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: excessive restriction)**: It removes risk by abandoning work requiring live lookups and does not satisfy the routine lookup need.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: Separating reads and writes satisfies (1) and (2), and the simple one-sentence standard also meets (3).

questions.title: Drive writes fail only in Enterprise despite identical configuration

Check whether the Enterprise administrator enabled Drive unified actions.

Have all users sign in to Drive again to refresh authentication.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: overengineering)**: Recreating an agent does not enable actions disabled by administrators.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: Enterprise defaults to disabled, so administrator enablement may be the cause.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: confusion between controls)**: Approval settings determine confirmation timing after an action is enabled; they do not enable it.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: approach for a different issue)**: Successful reading shows authentication is present; signing in again does not address the cause.

questions.title: Matching human confirmation to the type of task
questions.prompt: Match five customer-support agent tasks to confirmation methods based on reversibility and impact. Use each method once; **one is unused**.

options.text: Have a responsible person inspect and approve each action before execution.
Execute automatically without confirmation.
Allow execution and have a person review the result afterward.
Do not give the agent the tool; have a person perform the task directly.
Stop the agent’s response and hand the matter to a responsible person.
Collect all activity logs and review them together once a month.

items.text: Look up a customer’s order status: read-only, changing nothing.
Save a support-summary draft in an internal folder: it can be deleted or edited anytime, and staff can review and correct it later.
Send a compensation email to an external customer: it cannot be recalled.
Give final payment approval: policy permits only a person to do so.
Handle a customer demanding a compensation promise while mentioning a lawsuit: the agent must not make that commitment.

questions.explanation:
The criteria are reversibility and scope of impact. Anthropic encourages locally reversible actions and recommends asking before irreversible, destructive, or externally consequential actions. OpenAI similarly advises care with write approvals in workflows that send, edit, publish, or delete.

| Item | Match | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | {{option:b}} | A read-only lookup has no side effects and needs no confirmation. |
| 2 | {{option:c}} | This reversible internal write can be corrected later, so post-execution review is sufficient. |
| 3 | {{option:a}} | An external, unretractable message needs review before execution. |
| 4 | {{option:d}} | Policy reserves the decision for people, so the agent should not receive the tool. |
| 5 | {{option:e}} | A matter where the agent must not make commitments needs human ownership, not merely approval of a drafted commitment. Stop and escalate. |
| Unused | {{option:f}} | Monthly batch review cannot prevent irreversible actions and suits none of these tasks. |

**References**: [Prompting best practices › Balancing autonomy and safety](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices) · [ChatGPT Workspace Agents for Enterprise and Business › Manage write actions](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/20001143-chatgpt-workspace-agents-for-enterprise-and-business)

questions.title: Choosing an account for an inventory-lookup agent
questions.prompt:
A logistics team connects an internal inventory system to an agent used by 30 employees. The agent **only reads** inventory quantities. Requirements:

- (1) Account permissions are **limited to what lookup requires**.
- (2) The connection survives an employee’s **departure or transfer**.
- (3) The 30 employees need **no individual authentication**.

Which connection is most appropriate?

options.text: Use the inventory manager’s personal account with inventory-read permission only.
Have all 30 employees sign in with their own system accounts.
Use a service account with read and write permissions, disabling write tools in the agent’s tool list.
Create a read-only service account with only inventory-lookup permission and use it as a shared connection.

questions.explanation:
Requirements (1) and (2) are decisive. OpenAI distinguishes End-user account authentication, where every runner uses their own account, from Agent-owned account authentication, a shared agent connection. It recommends service accounts for shared connections where possible. Since only lookup is needed, least privilege also requires limiting the service account itself to read-only.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Permissions are narrow, but dependence on one person’s account risks disruption on departure or transfer, violating (2).
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Per-user accounts reduce dependence on one employee, but all 30 must authenticate, violating (3).
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It is stable and shared, but the account itself has write privileges, violating (1). Tool-setting changes could enable writing.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: A shared read-only service account satisfies all three requirements.

**References**: [ChatGPT Workspace Agents for Enterprise and Business › Choose an authentication type](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/20001143-chatgpt-workspace-agents-for-enterprise-and-business)

questions.title: Human confirmation points for a year-end tax inquiry agent
questions.prompt:
HR is building an agent for year-end tax inquiries. It reads employee submissions, drafts guidance, **edits and saves deduction items in the HR system on employees’ behalf**, and **transmits finalized filing information for submission to an external agency**. Confirmation points must:

- (1) Cover **every difficult-to-reverse step before execution**.
- (2) **Minimize confirmation fatigue** for employees and staff.
- (3) Form a list short enough for instructions.

Select TWO stages requiring confirmation.

options.text: Immediately before saving deduction changes on an employee’s behalf, summarize before-and-after values and obtain confirmation.
Before every lookup of submitted material, show the target and reason and request confirmation.
Every time guidance wording is revised, show the changed sentences and request confirmation.
Immediately before transmission to the external agency, summarize the destination and content and obtain confirmation.
Before every temporary draft save, show the location and content and request confirmation.

questions.explanation:
Requirements (1) and (2) are decisive. Anthropic recommends freely performing locally reversible work while asking before actions that are difficult to undo, affect shared systems, or are externally visible. Changing and saving records, and transmitting externally, therefore require confirmation.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: This write changes employee deduction records, and an incorrect save can propagate to other processing, so confirmation must precede execution.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Reading changes no state. Requiring confirmation works but violates (2).
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Wording can be revised again at any time, so repeated confirmation worsens (2) and (3).
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: Transmission to an external agency is difficult to reverse and externally visible, requiring prior confirmation.
- **{{option:E}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Temporary drafts can be overwritten or deleted. Repeated confirmation violates (2) and lengthens the list.

This question selects confirmation points; how to express the general confirmation rule in instructions is a separate design issue.

**References**: [Prompting best practices › Balancing autonomy and safety](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices)

questions.title: Stopping a shared agent producing incorrect email drafts at scale
questions.prompt:
A Gemini Enterprise company receives a report that an employee-built, team-shared Workflow Builder agent is generating many incorrect customer email drafts. Several other agents share its email and CRM connectors. The administrator needs a state change that:

- (1) **Immediately prevents ordinary users** from using it during investigation.
- (2) Preserves **owner and administrator access to configuration and history**.
- (3) Does **not delete** the agent.
- (4) Allows resumption **without rebuilding sharing settings**.
- (5) Leaves **other agents using the same connectors unaffected**.

Which action is most appropriate?

options.text: Delete the agent and recreate it from backed-up configuration after investigation.
Set the agent to Suspended, then restore Enabled after investigation.
Remove all shared users and groups, record the list, and reshare afterward.
Disable its email and CRM connectors organization-wide, then re-enable them after investigation.

questions.explanation:
Requirements (1), (2), and (3) are decisive. Gemini Enterprise documentation describes Suspended as temporarily inactive. The agent remains in the gallery with a notice, users cannot interact with it, and owners and administrators retain full access.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It blocks ordinary use but violates (3). Recreation does not retain sharing and history, also failing (2) and (4).
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: It immediately blocks use, retains privileged access, avoids deletion and sharing changes, and does not affect other agents, satisfying (1)–(5).
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It can block users but requires re-entering sharing targets and risks omissions, violating (4).
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It also stops other agents using those connectors, violating (5).

The documentation describes Disabled as an inactive state hidden from the gallery. It does not fully detail all differences, so this investigation scenario uses Suspended because owner and administrator access is explicitly documented.

**References**: [Gemini Enterprise agents overview › Agent states](https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini/enterprise/docs/agents-overview)

questions.title: Designing confirmation points for refund automation
questions.prompt:
An online store’s support team is introducing a refund agent. It receives about 1,500 requests daily, including about 150 for KRW 100,000 or more. Transferred refunds cannot be canceled. Four staff members can each review at most about 150 cases daily. Requirements:

- (1) Reduce incorrect payments because they are **unrecoverable losses**.
- (2) Approval waits must **not exceed 24 hours**.
- (3) Individual approval work must fit **staff capacity**.
- (4) Every refund is **logged for later audit**.

Which design is most appropriate?

options.text: Require individual prior approval for all refunds and have staff work nights if the queue grows.
Let the agent immediately process all refunds and have staff review every case the following day.
Bundle requests once daily for one batch approval, placing high-value cases at the top, then process the batch.
Automatically process refunds below KRW 100,000 with sampled later review, and require individual prior approval for refunds of KRW 100,000 or more.

questions.explanation:
Requirements (1), (2), and (3) are decisive; (4) is common to all designs. Irreversible writes call for prior confirmation, but approval for every case creates fatigue and delays. Concentrating individual prior approval on high-impact cases and sampled later review on lower-impact cases follows Anthropic’s reversibility-and-impact principle. This tradeoff still allows some incorrect payments below KRW 100,000 before review detects them.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It best protects (1), but four people cannot individually review 1,500 cases daily, violating (2) and (3).
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It satisfies (2) and (3) but identifies errors only after payment, failing to prevent unrecoverable loss under (1).
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It eases time constraints but removes individual review through batch approval, weakening protection against high-value losses.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: Four staff can individually review the 150 high-value cases, satisfying (2) and (3), while prior approval prevents larger losses. The tradeoff is accepting some small erroneous payments.

The amount threshold must be implemented in the refund system or business process. ChatGPT workspace agents’ Custom approval distinguishes write actions, not monetary amounts.

**References**: [Prompting best practices › Balancing autonomy and safety](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices) · [ChatGPT Workspace Agents for Enterprise and Business › Manage write actions](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/20001143-chatgpt-workspace-agents-for-enterprise-and-business)

questions.title: Evaluating statements about Claude remote MCP connectors
questions.prompt: An operations lead at a company using Claude Team sends a remote MCP adoption memo to the tool coordinator. Mark Yes if each statement agrees with Anthropic’s official documentation and No if any part is incorrect.

items.text: On Team, only an Owner or Primary Owner can add an organization custom connector, and members must each select Connect before using it.
When a registered custom connector’s server URL changes, edit only the URL in settings; removal and re-addition are unnecessary.
Advanced Research cannot call tools from local MCP servers.
Remote MCP connections originate from Anthropic’s cloud rather than the user’s device, so a server behind a firewall must allowlist Anthropic’s IP ranges.

questions.explanation:
This question covers who adds remote custom connectors, how connector details change, and where connections originate. Statement 3 concerns the server types Research can use. Only one statement is incorrect because it changes a documented condition.

1. **Yes**: On Team and Enterprise, only Owners or Primary Owners add organization custom connectors, and members must still individually select Connect afterward.
2. **No**: Connector details cannot be edited in place. The documentation directs users to remove the connector and add it again with the new information.
3. **Yes**: Advanced Research explicitly cannot call tools on local MCP servers.
4. **Yes**: Remote connections originate from Anthropic’s cloud, so private or firewalled servers must allow Anthropic’s IP ranges.

questions.title: An email-sending workflow requiring human confirmation
questions.prompt: Customer support is introducing a workflow where an agent prepares customer emails and a staff member approves before sending. Sending cannot be undone, and sending history supports later audits. Arrange the steps, including preparation before production, according to their **dependencies**.

items.text: Have staff review the draft, revise if needed, and approve it.
Send the approved draft to the customer.
Deploy the validated workflow, receive real customer requests, and create and save drafts without sending.
Record the approving staff member and the sending result.
Configure the sending tool to require approval before execution.
Run a test request with an internal recipient and verify that sending cannot occur before approval.

questions.explanation:
Irreversible sending must use a human-approved result as input, and the approval mechanism must be configured and tested before real customer requests arrive. These dependencies determine the order. Anthropic recommends user confirmation before difficult-to-reverse external sending.

| Order | Step | Dependency | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | (5) Require approval | Establish the control first so every later send passes through it. | External sending needs prior confirmation. |
| 2 | (6) Run an internal test | A configured control is needed to verify that sending cannot occur before approval. | Validate internally before involving real customers. |
| 3 | (3) Deploy, receive requests, and save drafts | The scenario requires validated deployment before real requests. Saving unsent drafts is reversible. | Temporary saving is reversible. |
| 4 | (1) Review and approve | A draft must exist to review. | Confirm before external sending. |
| 5 | (2) Send | The approved final draft determines what to send. | Irreversible external actions follow confirmation. |
| 6 | (4) Record | The approver and send outcome can be recorded once sending is complete. | The send result is input. |

This is a general product-independent sequence. Approval mechanisms differ by product, such as Always ask for write actions, so consult the relevant help.

**References**: [Prompting best practices › Balancing autonomy and safety](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices) · [ChatGPT Workspace Agents for Enterprise and Business › Manage write actions](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/20001143-chatgpt-workspace-agents-for-enterprise-and-business)

questions.title: Separating directory-publishing permissions for employee-built agents
questions.prompt:
An HR operations coordinator in ChatGPT Enterprise wants a group of team tool coordinators to create workspace agents and publish them to the workspace directory. Their RBAC role must:

- (1) Let employees **create and edit agents themselves**.
- (2) Let them **publish directly to the directory**, without administrator delegation.
- (3) Prevent them from publishing agents using **personal or shared authenticated connections**, which require separate review.

Select TWO permissions.

options.text: Enable agent building
Enable agent publishing
Enable agent publishing with agent-owned connections
Grant only Enable agents; HR operations builds agents on employees’ behalf.
Grant only Enable agent building; HR operations publishes on employees’ behalf.

questions.explanation:
All three requirements are decisive. OpenAI separates building, directory publishing, and publishing agents with authenticated connections into distinct permissions. Building includes creating, editing, and duplicating; publishing enables directory listing; publishing agents with personal or shared authenticated connections requires the separate final permission. That permission carries a warning that other people may use the builder’s account.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: It satisfies self-service creation and editing in (1).
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: It satisfies direct directory publishing in (2), while withholding the connection-specific permission preserves (3).
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It permits publishing authenticated-connection agents, violating (3).
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Employees can only run agents, violating (1) and increasing the coordinator’s work.
- **{{option:E}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Employees can build but rely on delegated publishing, violating (2).

Permission names and interfaces can change; check the current help before assigning them.

**References**: [ChatGPT Workspace Agents for Enterprise and Business › Who can create and publish agents](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/20001143-chatgpt-workspace-agents-for-enterprise-and-business)

questions.title: Auditing employees’ connected-app activity
questions.prompt:
An audit team in a ChatGPT Enterprise workspace wants to inspect external apps employees use through ChatGPT. Requirements:

- (1) Inspect records of **app requests and related responses**.
- (2) Inspect **account connection and disconnection history**.
- (3) Do **not depend on employee cooperation**.
- (4) Do **not interrupt app use** for the audit.

Which approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Query app-call and app-authentication connection/disconnection records in Compliance Platform.
Download agent user counts and run counts from Analytics and compare them.
Ask employees to inspect their own Settings > Apps connection status and submit it.
Temporarily disable the app and reconstruct usage from employee inquiries.

questions.explanation:
Requirements (1) and (2) are decisive. OpenAI help states that app calls are recorded in the OpenAI Compliance Logs platform. App activity records may contain requests and related response information, while app-authentication records may include account connection and disconnection events. Compliance Platform is available to eligible Enterprise and Edu workspaces.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: Administrative inspection covers both record types without employee assistance or interrupting the app.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: confusion between features)**: Analytics provides agent-user and run counts, not request/response records or connection history.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It shows connection status but depends on employee submissions, violating (3), and contains no request/response records.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Disabling is available but violates (4); reconstructing use from inquiries is not examining logs.

The documentation says ChatGPT Business administrators do not automatically access members’ ordinary private conversations. Compliance Platform is limited to eligible Enterprise and Edu workspaces.
