questions.title: What to do before shortening retention
questions.prompt:
A Claude Enterprise Owner plans to reduce retention for a shared HR project containing chats from 180 days to 90 days. Its last update was four months ago. Individual-chat retention is configured separately. Requirements:

- (1) The HR project and **all its chats** follow 90-day retention.
- (2) Preserve audit material **before deletion**.
- (3) Retain the project’s **sharing configuration and team access**.

Which sequence is most appropriate?

options.text: Leave the project at 180 days, shorten only non-project individual chats to 90 days, and leave audit material in place.
Save 90-day project retention first and request recovery if needed material is deleted.
Export and separately preserve audit material first, then save 90-day project retention.
Create a new project and move needed material, shorten the old project to 90 days, and reshare the new project.

questions.explanation:
Requirements (1) and (2) are decisive. Claude help says project retention overrides chat retention within it and is measured from the project’s last update, including chat creation or knowledge changes. Shortening retention immediately deletes data outside the new period when saved, and deletion cannot be reversed.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Project settings override contained-chat settings, leaving those chats under 180 days and violating (1).
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: The setting applies, but immediate irreversible deletion violates (2).
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: Exporting first preserves needed material under (2), while using the existing project maintains (1) and (3).
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Material is preserved, but sharing must be rebuilt for the new project, violating (3). The new project also falls under the same retention settings.

Custom retention is Enterprise-only with a 30-day minimum. Months are calculated as 30 days, so a project last updated four months (120 days) ago becomes eligible for deletion under 90-day retention.

**References**: [Custom data retention controls for Enterprise plans](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/10440198-custom-data-retention-controls-for-enterprise-plans)

questions.title: Automatic access removal after transfers or departures
questions.prompt:
A Claude Enterprise HR team has a sensitive project containing evaluation criteria and examples. The administrator can enable “Share resources with this group” for the relevant group. Requirements:

- (1) Access **automatically disappears** after transfer or departure.
- (2) The coordinator does **not manually revoke each person**.
- (3) The project is **not organization-public**.

Which setup is most appropriate?

options.text: Invite each teammate individually and have the coordinator review and revoke access quarterly.
Keep the project private and share it with the HR group so membership determines access.
Make the project organization-public while keeping sensitive chats private.
Give the team leader Can edit access and have them manually revoke access after each transfer or departure.

questions.explanation:
Requirements (1) and (2) are decisive. Claude’s Enterprise group sharing beta follows group membership. Members leaving a group lose access through that group unless another access path exists. Administrators must enable sharing in group settings before it is available.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It requires manual inspection, and access remains until review, violating (1) and (2).
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: Access follows group changes, satisfying (1) and (2), while private visibility satisfies (3). The tradeoff is reliance on a beta feature.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Chats are private by default, but public-project knowledge and instructions remain organization-visible, violating (3).
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: The leader can revoke access but must do so individually, violating (2).

An alternate access path, such as an individual invitation, can preserve access after group removal. Check that individual invitations have not been mixed into the group-based setup.

**References**: [Manage project visibility and sharing › Group sharing](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/9519189-manage-project-visibility-and-sharing) · [Manage project visibility and sharing › Remove access](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/9519189-manage-project-visibility-and-sharing)

questions.title: Defining source scope for a payroll-inquiry assistant
questions.prompt:
HR is creating a shared-project assistant for eight support staff answering payroll-policy inquiries. These staff **cannot view other employees’ original payroll records**. Using the full payroll table would produce the most accurate answers. About 20% of inquiries need exact individual amounts and can be handled separately by HR. Requirements:

- (1) The **eight support staff themselves** use the assistant.
- (2) Other employees’ **original payroll records remain hidden** from them.
- (3) Preserve policy-answer **accuracy as much as possible**.
- (4) Manage and audit access and knowledge configuration in **one place**.

Which setup is most appropriate?

options.text: Use one private project shared only with the eight-person group, uploading salary ranges by grade and policy excerpts, and route individual-amount questions to HR.
Upload the full payroll table to a project shared with the eight-person group and instruct it not to reveal original payroll records.
Have only the HR head use a private project containing the full table and relay the eight staff members’ questions and answers.
Have each of the eight staff create a private project with relevant excerpts and route individual-amount questions to HR.

questions.explanation:
Requirements (2) and (4) are decisive; the tradeoff is exposure prevention versus accuracy. The correct choice sacrifices part of (3). OpenAI help says shared-project responses use uploaded files and directly shared content, and members can view project files. Claude likewise supports private invited-member projects and group sharing. Material that members must not read should therefore not enter shared knowledge. Minimal excerpts shift individual-payroll questions to manual HR handling and slow those responses.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: One project centralizes access and knowledge, satisfying (1), (2), and (4). The tradeoff is that the assistant cannot directly answer individual-amount questions, partly sacrificing (3).
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Accuracy may be high, but instructions are not access controls and members can open uploaded files, violating (2).
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It protects originals, preserves accuracy, and centralizes material, but only the HR head uses the assistant, violating (1).
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Excerpts protect records, but eight separate projects prevent one-place configuration and auditing, violating (4).

**References**: [Projects in ChatGPT › Can ChatGPT's responses in shared projects include private or internal data?](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/10169521-projects-in-chatgpt) · [Manage project visibility and sharing › Understand the two project visibility options](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/9519189-manage-project-visibility-and-sharing)

questions.title: Evaluating administrator controls and sharing scope
questions.prompt: A team tool coordinator is reviewing notes about administrator controls across three providers. Mark Yes if a statement agrees with the relevant official documentation and No if any part is incorrect.

items.text: In Google Workspace, disabling Gemini in Drive still allows users to ask Gemini in Gmail about Drive files.
ChatGPT Business administrators manage workspace settings and app availability but do not automatically access members’ ordinary private conversations.
When organizational-unit and configuration-group settings differ for the same Google Workspace user, organizational-unit settings take precedence.
Unified Google Drive actions are disabled in ChatGPT Enterprise until administrators enable them, while Business enables them by default.

questions.explanation:
These statements cover separate facts: disabling service-specific features, administrator access, precedence of overlapping settings, and plan-specific Google Drive action defaults. One statement reverses a documented condition.

1. **Yes**: Google explains that disabling Gemini in one service does not prevent another service’s Gemini from accessing that service’s data, giving Gmail questions about Drive files as an example.
2. **Yes**: OpenAI says Business administrators manage workspace settings and app availability but do not automatically access members’ ordinary private conversations.
3. **No**: Google permits settings by organizational unit or configuration group, and group settings override organizational-unit settings. The statement reverses precedence.
4. **Yes**: Unified Google Drive actions are disabled in Enterprise and Edu until enabled by administrators, but enabled by default in Business. New Enterprise and Edu workspaces may start with some apps enabled, so “all new apps are disabled” would be inaccurate.

Statement 1 means service-specific Gemini settings do not block every data-access path. Source sharing permissions remain the primary access control.

**References**: [Manage access to Gemini features in Workspace services › Data access note](https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/gemini/manage-access-to-gemini-features-in-workspace-services) · [Admin controls, security, and compliance for plugins and apps › Compliance](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/11509118-admin-controls-security-and-compliance-in-connectors-enterprise-edu-and-business) · [Manage access to Gemini features in Workspace services › Scope by organizational unit or group](https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/gemini/manage-access-to-gemini-features-in-workspace-services) · [Admin controls, security, and compliance for plugins and apps › Default settings](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/11509118-admin-controls-security-and-compliance-in-connectors-enterprise-edu-and-business)

questions.title: Blocking gemini.google.com while retaining Gemini in Gmail and Docs
questions.prompt:
A Google Workspace administrator wants to block direct access to gemini.google.com while retaining Gemini inside Gmail and Docs. Some services have configuration-group exceptions. Requirements:

- (1) Block **gemini.google.com through a control**, not an announcement.
- (2) **Keep Gemini available inside Gmail and Docs**.
- (3) **Verify intended service settings** after the change.

Select TWO actions.

options.text: Tell employees not to use gemini.google.com and address violations individually.
Turn off Gemini app access for gemini.google.com and leave service-specific Gemini settings unchanged.
Disable Gemini in Gmail, Docs, and Drive through service panels, leaving app access enabled.
Separately inspect Gmail and Docs in the Feature access panel, including group exceptions.
After disabling app access, disable Gemini in every service and then re-enable only required services.

questions.explanation:
Requirements (1) and (3) are decisive. Google documents Gemini app access as a separate toggle from service-specific Gemini controls. Disabling app access does not affect other AI features within Workspace services. Feature access can be set organization-wide, by OU, or by configuration group, with group settings overriding OU settings.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: An announcement is not an access control, violating (1).
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: It blocks only app access while preserving in-service Gemini, satisfying (1) and (2).
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It disables the required service features, violating (2), while leaving gemini.google.com available, failing (1).
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: Independent service controls and group precedence require separate verification to satisfy (3).
- **{{option:E}} (Incorrect: overengineering)**: It changes service settings twice and may disturb existing group exceptions, expanding the change and verification burden unnecessarily.

Feature access requires the Gemini Settings administrator privilege and is available only in some editions. Users also need smart features and personalization enabled to use Gemini.

**References**: [Manage access to Gemini features in Workspace services › Gemini app toggle](https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/gemini/manage-access-to-gemini-features-in-workspace-services) · [Manage access to Gemini features in Workspace services › Gemini controls in Workspace services](https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/gemini/manage-access-to-gemini-features-in-workspace-services)

questions.title: Handling Gemini Notebook data after activity deletion
questions.prompt:
A Google Workspace administrator responds to employee privacy deletion requests by turning off Keep Activity and deleting existing Gemini Apps activity. Those employees also use Gemini Notebook. Remaining requirements:

- (1) Delete the requesting employees’ **notebooks and sources**.
- (2) The coordinator **checks for and deletes notebook Gemini conversations remaining in the Gemini app**.
- (3) Leave nonrequesting employees’ notebooks and conversations **unaffected**.

Which action is most appropriate?

options.text: Delete those employees’ Gemini Apps activity again, leave Keep Activity off, and report completion.
Delete their notebooks and sources, then tell interested employees to delete remaining conversations themselves.
Delete their notebooks in Gemini Notebook, then check the app conversation list for associated Gemini conversations and delete them.
Tell everyone in the department to delete notebooks and app conversations so no requester is missed.

questions.explanation:
Requirements (1) and (2) are decisive; each distractor violates one of (1)–(3). Google explains that turning off Keep Activity or deleting Gemini Apps activity does not delete Gemini Notebook data. Deleting a notebook removes it and its sources, but associated Gemini conversations return to the main conversation list and must be managed separately in the Gemini app.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Activity deletion executes but does not affect notebook data, failing (1).
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Notebook data is deleted, but remaining-conversation verification and deletion are left to employee choice rather than the coordinator, violating (2).
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: It handles notebook/source data and remaining app conversations in their respective locations, only for requesters, satisfying (3) too.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It also deletes nonrequesters’ material, violating (3).

Notebook Gemini conversations are stored according to Keep Activity. A notebook containing Gemini conversations remains private and cannot be shared.

**References**: [Notebooks in Gemini Apps › Keep Activity and Gemini Notebook](https://support.google.com/gemininotebook/answer/17003757) · [Notebooks in Gemini Apps › Delete a notebook](https://support.google.com/gemininotebook/answer/17003757)

questions.title: Controlling sharing of employee-built agents
questions.prompt: Which administrative setup **simultaneously** meets [Requirement 1] and [Security]?
questions.context:
**[Company]** Haesol Finance uses Gemini Enterprise. Twelve risk-team employees build their own work agents in Workflow Builder without coding.

**[Existing environment]** An employee-built “Suspicious Transaction Memo” agent compares suspected transactions’ facts with policy documents, drafts memos, and notifies the responsible channel. Administrators preprovisioned the policy repository and notification-channel connectors. The employee who built the agent remains its owner and continues editing it directly.

**[Requirement 1]** Preserve employee self-service creation while allowing completed agents to be shared with teams and groups. Administrators want review and approval before employee-built agents are shared.

**[Requirement 2]** Before publishing, simulate 20 representative inputs, assess quality, and fix each failure type at its source. Testing must finish before publication.

**[Security]** Employees may use only the administrator-provided policy repository and notification-channel connectors.

**[Note]** One employee proposes reusing existing Gems unchanged. Another suggests upgrading the model. A third proposes migrating the entire policy repository to a new repository.

options.text: Disable employee agent creation and have the risk-team administrator build and share agents on request.
Allow unrestricted sharing and have administrators review shared agents weekly and remove problematic shares.
Transfer ownership of completed agents to administrators for review and sharing.
Require administrator review and approval for employee agent sharing, and limit available connectors and tools to provisioned ones.

questions.explanation:
The decisive requirements are retaining self-service creation, reviewing before sharing, and the security boundary. Gemini Enterprise administrators can require review and approval for sharing employee-built agents. Workflow Builder allows employee creation, while available actions and tools remain limited to administrator-provisioned connectors, tools, and permissions.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It simplifies review but removes self-service creation, violating [Requirement 1].
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It preserves autonomy but reviews after sharing rather than before, violating [Requirement 1].
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Review precedes sharing, but changed ownership conflicts with the employee continuing to edit directly in [Existing environment], and adds administrative work for every agent.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: It retains employee creation while enforcing pre-sharing approval and provisioned-connector limits.

The suggestion to reuse Gems is a distractor unrelated to these requirements. Sharing-approval setting names and locations may vary by edition; check the current administration interface.

**References**: [Gemini Enterprise agents overview › Sharing](https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini/enterprise/docs/agents-overview) · [Workflow Builder overview › Agent controls and security](https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini/enterprise/docs/workflow-builder)

questions.title: Choosing repair locations from simulation results
questions.prompt:
Simulation of the 20 representative inputs under [Requirement 2] reveals three failure types:

- (1) Two fabricated figures: limits absent from policy documents.
- (2) Four answers omit required rules: the rules exist in the repository but are outside the agent’s reading scope.
- (3) Five notification-format errors: the content is correct.

Which method **fixes each cause at its source and verifies improvement before publication**?
questions.context:
**[Company]** Haesol Finance uses Gemini Enterprise. Twelve risk-team employees build their own work agents in Workflow Builder without coding.

**[Existing environment]** An employee-built “Suspicious Transaction Memo” agent compares suspected transactions’ facts with policy documents, drafts memos, and notifies the responsible channel. Administrators preprovisioned the policy repository and notification-channel connectors. The employee who built the agent remains its owner and continues editing it directly.

**[Requirement 1]** Preserve employee self-service creation while allowing completed agents to be shared with teams and groups. Administrators want review and approval before employee-built agents are shared.

**[Requirement 2]** Before publishing, simulate 20 representative inputs, assess quality, and fix each failure type at its source. Testing must finish before publication.

**[Security]** Employees may use only the administrator-provided policy repository and notification-channel connectors.

**[Note]** One employee proposes reusing existing Gems unchanged. Another suggests upgrading the model. A third proposes migrating the entire policy repository to a new repository.

options.text: (1) Instruct it to say when information is absent; (2) emphasize “Cite every rule” in instructions; (3) fix the notification step’s output format; rerun the same 20 inputs.
(1) Instruct it to say when information is absent; (2) add missing rules to the agent’s readable document scope; (3) fix the notification step’s output format; rerun the same 20 inputs.
(1) Instruct it to say when information is absent; (2) add missing rules to the readable scope; (3) fix notification output format; rerun only the 11 failed cases.
(1) Instruct it to say when information is absent; (2) add missing rules to the readable scope; (3) fix notification output format; publish and assess improvement through user reports.

questions.explanation:
[Requirement 2] demands fixing each failure type at its source and finishing checks before publication. Fabrication calls for instructions governing absent evidence; omission calls for correcting readable source scope; formatting belongs in the output-producing step. Workflow Builder supports preview and simulation in an integrated test environment before publication. Rerunning the entire same input set checks both repaired cases and previously passing cases.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: confusion between repair locations)**: Missing rules are outside reading scope. Instruction emphasis cannot make unavailable source content appear.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: It fixes each cause in the appropriate location and compares all 20 inputs before publication.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Repair locations are correct, but retesting only 11 failures cannot detect regressions in the nine previously passing cases.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Repair locations are correct, but post-publication reports violate pre-publication testing and may send faulty notifications into real work.

Model upgrades and whole-repository migration are distractors that expand changes without isolating causes. The failure-to-repair mapping is a general diagnostic principle, not a table explicitly prescribed by the cited document.

**References**: [Workflow Builder overview › Testing and simulation before publishing](https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini/enterprise/docs/workflow-builder)

questions.title: Choosing how to grade representative answers
questions.prompt:
A quotation-guidance team compares instruction revisions using 200 representative questions. Each answer must match source-table unit prices and clause numbers and use a polite customer-facing tone. One coordinator grades every revision. Requirements:

- (1) Finish **within one day**, repeatably after every revision.
- (2) Give the **same judgment for the same answer**.
- (3) Record tone as **pass/fail** too.
- (4) Accept **equivalent meaning despite different wording**.

Select TWO appropriate grading methods.

options.text: Have the coordinator read all 200 answers and manually score prices, numbers, and tone from 1–5.
Automatically compare unit prices and clause numbers with source-table values and return pass/fail.
Have AI grade tone pass/fail using “Pass if the answer leaves a good impression on the customer.”
Have AI grade tone pass/fail using “Use polite language and include a greeting in the first sentence.”
Automatically compare prices, numbers, and tone with exact model-answer sentences and return pass/fail.

questions.explanation:
All four requirements are decisive. Anthropic recommends the fastest reliable, scalable grading method. Code-based grading is fastest and most reliable but weak on nuance. AI grading is flexible when supplied detailed, clear rubrics and empirically checkable outputs such as correct/incorrect. Human grading is slow and expensive and should be avoided where possible.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Manual grading can work, but repeatedly completing 200 answers in one day is difficult, violating (1). Undefined scoring also weakens (2) and (3).
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: Deterministic value matching is fastest through automated rules and gives consistent judgments.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: AI can finish quickly and produce pass/fail, but “good impression” is not an observable condition and may yield different judgments for the same answer, violating (2).
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: Observable criteria make AI grading suitable for nuanced tone while meeting (1)–(4).
- **{{option:E}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It is automatic, consistent, and binary, but exact-sentence matching rejects equivalent wording, violating (4).

**References**: [Define success criteria and build evaluations › Grading evals](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/develop-tests)
tags: Choosing how to grade representative answers

questions.title: Building an initial representative question set
questions.prompt:
Before launching a support assistant, one coordinator is creating the first representative question set for reuse after every instruction change. Requirements:

- (1) Its composition resembles **actual incoming inquiries**.
- (2) It exposes **likely failure points**.
- (3) It contains **about 30 questions** and is created **within one day**.

Select TWO necessary components.

options.text: Count inquiry types in the past month’s logs and sample questions in those proportions.
Include some questions with no answer in the sources and exceptions to the rules.
Focus on questions the assistant already answers well to make existing-quality preservation easy to observe.
Automatically collect more than 300 logged questions to improve reliability.
Create only questions from the coordinator’s strongest subject area where answers can be graded confidently.

questions.explanation:
Requirements (1) and (2) are decisive. Anthropic recommends matching evaluations to real-work question distributions and including edge cases such as nonexistent input data. More questions can help when automated grading is available, but this scenario limits the set to about 30 and creation to one day.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: Proportional sampling reflects the actual distribution under (1) and can fit about 30 questions.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: Missing-answer and exception cases expose likely failures, satisfying (2).
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It checks retained quality but underrepresents likely failures, violating (2).
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: More questions may help evaluation, but exceed the size and preparation limits in (3).
- **{{option:E}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It eases grading but biases coverage toward one person’s expertise rather than real inquiries, violating (1).

**References**: [Define success criteria and build evaluations › Eval design principles](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/develop-tests)
tags: Building an initial representative question set

questions.title: Choosing evaluation dimensions for release criteria
questions.prompt:
HR is launching a shared policy-inquiry assistant and already has representative questions. Release requires answers matching policy, consistent answers to paraphrases, and compliance with instructions not to disclose other employees’ personal information. Requirements:

- (1) Verify **all three**.
- (2) Identify shortfalls **by dimension**.
- (3) Do **not measure unrelated dimensions** for this release.

Which evaluation setup is most appropriate?

options.text: Set a target only for policy agreement, excluding consistency and privacy-instruction compliance.
Set separate targets for policy agreement, consistency, and privacy-instruction compliance, measure the same question set, and record each dimension.
Add tone, response speed, and call cost to the three dimensions and set targets for all six.
Inspect all three but assign each answer one overall 1–10 score and pass if the average is at least 8.

questions.explanation:
All three requirements are decisive. Anthropic explains that most use cases need multidimensional evaluation across several success criteria. Common dimensions include task fidelity, consistency, tone, privacy, context utilization, latency, and price. Criteria must be specific, measurable, and relevant to the application’s purpose, with separate targets for each.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It is simple and separately recorded but omits consistency and privacy compliance, violating (1).
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: Separate targets cover all required dimensions, separate records identify shortfalls, and no unrelated dimensions are measured.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: These are legitimate common criteria, but tone, speed, and cost are outside this release’s requirements, violating (3).
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: A combined score hides which dimension failed, violating (2).

**References**: [Define success criteria and build evaluations › Common success criteria](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/develop-tests) · [Define success criteria and build evaluations › Build strong criteria](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/develop-tests)

questions.title: Writing measurable release-pass criteria
questions.prompt:
A support team is defining release criteria for 30 refund-guidance questions. The assistant currently answers about 20 correctly in human reviewers’ judgment. It has two weeks to improve instructions and sources, with an expected maximum improvement of 5–7 questions. Criteria must:

- (1) Produce **the same pass/fail result across graders**.
- (2) Be **directly relevant to refund accuracy**.
- (3) Be **achievable within two weeks**.

Which criterion is most appropriate?

options.text: In at least 27 of 30 answers, the refund period and amount match the terms table, and the conclusion appears in the first sentence.
All 30 refund answers are satisfactory and easy for customers to understand.
At least 27 of 30 answers are no longer than 500 characters and contain no emoji.
In all 30 answers, the refund period and amount match the terms table, and the conclusion appears in the first sentence.

questions.explanation:
All three requirements are decisive. Anthropic recommends specific, measurable, achievable, relevant success criteria, using observable conditions and numbers instead of vague phrases such as “good performance.”

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: Matching periods and amounts and locating the conclusion are consistently observable, relevant to refunds, and a rise from 20 to 27 fits the expected improvement.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: The count and subject are clear, but “satisfactory and easy to understand” varies by grader, violating (1).
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It is observable and achievable, but length and emoji do not measure refund accuracy, violating (2).
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It is observable and relevant, but improvement from 20 to all 30 exceeds the expected range, violating (3).

The target count can be adjusted later using results from real inquiries after launch.

**References**: [Define success criteria and build evaluations › Build strong criteria](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/develop-tests)

questions.title: Prioritizing fixes before a fixed launch date
questions.prompt:
A customer-guidance assistant must launch in three days. Thirty representative questions reveal:

- Two hallucinations giving customers incorrect fees.
- Three omissions of necessary guidance.
- Eight formatting errors with correct content.

One person has a total of two days for fixes and retesting. Fixing one failure type takes about half a day, and rerunning the same 30 questions also takes half a day. Combining fixes still costs half a day per type. Requirements:

- (1) **Meet the launch date**.
- (2) Fix **failures directly harming customers before launch**.
- (3) Retest all 30 **after each individual fix** to identify which change causes regressions.
- (4) Track remaining issues in a **post-launch improvement list**.

Which plan is most appropriate?

options.text: Fix formatting and retest, fix omissions and retest, then launch with hallucinations on the post-launch list.
Fix hallucinations, omissions, and formatting sequentially, retesting after each, then launch once all are complete.
Fix all three types together, retest all 30 once, then launch.
Fix hallucinations and retest, fix omissions and retest, then launch with formatting errors on the post-launch list.

questions.explanation:
Requirements (1)–(3) are decisive, with the correct answer accepting a tradeoff under (4). Each fix plus retest takes one day, allowing two cycles in the available two days. Fixing hallucinations and omissions separately addresses greater customer harm and checks regressions after each change. Lower-impact formatting issues wait until after launch. This tests general prioritization rather than a single prescribed rule in official documentation.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It fits the schedule and retests, but leaves the most harmful hallucinations at launch, violating (2).
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Three fixes plus three retests take three days, exceeding the two available and jeopardizing (1).
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Three fixes plus one retest fit two days, but combined changes obscure which caused a regression, violating (3).
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: It meets (1)–(3), accepting eight remaining formatting errors and tracking them under (4).

**References**: General prioritization principles—customer harm first and retesting after each change—rather than a directly cited official document.

questions.title: JIT operations to free a departing employee’s Claude Team seat
questions.prompt:
Hanbit Accounting uses Claude Team and has configured SSO and JIT provisioning (creating an account on first sign-in) with its internal identity provider (IdP). It wants to transfer a recently departed employee's seat to a new hire. The requirements are:

- (1) Free the departed employee's seat for the new hire.
- (2) Prevent the departed employee from signing in through SSO and rejoining the organization.
- (3) Keep the Team plan and resolve this without purchasing additional features.

What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Only remove the departed employee's Anthropic app assignment in the IdP. Blocking sign-in automatically frees the seat as well.
Only remove the departed employee from the Claude organization's member list. The IdP settings will block subsequent sign-ins.
Remove the departed employee from the Claude organization's member list and also remove their Anthropic app assignment in the IdP.
Enable SCIM provisioning so removing the user in the IdP automatically removes them from Claude.

questions.explanation:
The relevant clues are requirements (1) and (2), along with "Claude Team plan" and "JIT." Claude's help article explains that JIT provisioning is available for Team, Enterprise, and Console organizations, creates an account when an assigned user first signs in, and consumes one seat per new member. It also states, "JIT never removes members automatically." Removing the IdP app assignment blocks sign-in, but the user remains on the member list and continues occupying a seat. Removing them only from Claude allows them to be added again at their next SSO sign-in. Permanent removal therefore requires two steps: removing them from Claude and unassigning them in the IdP.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect, factual error)**: Unassigning blocks sign-in, but the member entry and seat remain until an administrator removes them, violating (1).
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect, violates a constraint)**: The seat is freed, but if the IdP assignment remains, the departed employee is added again on SSO sign-in, violating (2).
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: Removal in Claude frees the seat, and removing the IdP assignment prevents rejoining, meeting (1)–(3).
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect, violates a constraint)**: SCIM automatically removes users removed from the IdP, but is unavailable on the Team plan, violating (3).

Additional note: On the Enterprise plan, SCIM can reduce these two steps to a single removal in the IdP (see WFA-N2 and WFA-N3). When JIT is used with group mappings, users removed from every mapped group are removed on their next sign-in, but users whose app assignment itself is removed still need administrator removal.

**Source documents**: [Set up JIT or SCIM provisioning (Claude) › Provisioning options · JIT deprovisioning](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/13133195-set-up-jit-or-scim-provisioning)

questions.title: Evaluating statements about SSO, SCIM, and deprovisioning across three providers
questions.prompt:
A team tools administrator summarizes identity integration notes from three providers' administrator documentation. Mark each statement Yes if it agrees with the relevant official documentation, or No if any part conflicts.

1. In ChatGPT Enterprise, SCIM (automatic synchronization of members and groups) can be configured independently of SSO (the sign-in method).
2. Deprovisioning a member through SCIM in ChatGPT also deletes that person's OpenAI account and personal workspace.
3. With SCIM in Claude Enterprise, users removed from the IdP's Anthropic app are automatically removed from the organization.
4. In Gemini Enterprise, one identity provider type is selected per supported location.

items.text: In ChatGPT Enterprise, SCIM (automatic synchronization of members and groups) can be configured independently of SSO (the sign-in method).
Deprovisioning a member through SCIM in ChatGPT also deletes that person's OpenAI account and personal workspace.
With SCIM in Claude Enterprise, users removed from the IdP's Anthropic app are automatically removed from the organization.
In Gemini Enterprise, one identity provider type is selected per supported location.

questions.explanation:
The four statements test separate facts: the division of responsibilities between SSO and SCIM, the scope of deprovisioning, automatic removal through SCIM, and the unit at which an identity provider is selected. One statement is false, created by changing one condition in the documentation. The key distinction is that SSO controls "how people sign in," while SCIM controls "who exists and in which groups (provisioning)."

| Number | Judgment | Rationale |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Yes | OpenAI's help article distinguishes "SCIM manages provisioning; single sign-on (SSO) manages how people authenticate" and explains, "You can configure SCIM independently of SSO." |
| 2 | No | OpenAI's help article states, "Deprovisioning a ChatGPT workspace member does not delete the person's OpenAI account or personal workspace." Only workspace membership is removed; the account is not deleted. |
| 3 | Yes | Claude's help article says that with SCIM, "Users removed from your IdP app are automatically removed." SCIM is available for Enterprise and Console organizations. |
| 4 | Yes | Gemini Enterprise documentation states, "You can select one identity provider type per location supported in Gemini Enterprise." Google Identity is recommended, and external IdPs connect through Workforce Identity Federation. |

Additional note: The standalone ChatGPT Business plan does not include SCIM, so another member-management method is required. The same help article warns that disabling a user in the IdP may leave their app assignment and access in place (see WFA-N11).

**Source documents**: [SCIM provisioning and management (ChatGPT) › SSO and SCIM · Deprovisioning](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/10011769-scim-provisioning-and-management) · [Set up JIT or SCIM provisioning (Claude) › Provisioning options](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/13133195-set-up-jit-or-scim-provisioning) · [Configure identity provider (Gemini Enterprise)](https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini/enterprise/docs/configure-identity-provider)

questions.title: The sequence for mapping IdP groups to Claude roles
questions.prompt:
Nuri Logistics uses Claude Enterprise and has already configured SSO and SCIM. Its IT administrator wants to enable group mappings so members of the IdP's "Finance" group automatically receive a custom Claude role (a finance-specific permission set). The requirements are:

- (1) When an employee changes groups in the IdP, their Claude role must change automatically.
- (2) No employee should be left without permissions when mappings are enabled.
- (3) Retain SCIM rather than switching to JIT.

Which sequence is most appropriate?

options.text: Save the SCIM settings with group mappings enabled, then assign custom roles to the groups after synchronization finishes.
Save with group mappings disabled and complete the first synchronization; assign the synchronized groups to custom roles under Roles in organization settings, then enable group mappings.
Manually create groups in Claude with the same names as the IdP groups and add members, then switch to JIT and enable group mappings.
Leave group mappings disabled and use SCIM only to create accounts; have an administrator manually change Claude roles whenever employees change groups.

questions.explanation:
The relevant clues are requirements (1)–(3). In role-based access control (RBAC), permissions are bundled into roles rather than assigned individually to people, and group mappings connect IdP groups to those roles (role mapping). Claude's help article specifies the sequence for combining SCIM with custom roles. First save with group mappings disabled and complete the initial synchronization (IdP groups do not appear in Claude until the first SCIM sync). Next, assign the synchronized groups to custom roles under Roles in Organization settings, then enable group mappings on the user-provisioning screen. Users mapped to groups without custom-role assignments have no permissions, leaving features hidden or disabled.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Enabling mappings first leaves users without permissions until roles are assigned, violating (2).
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: Assigning roles to groups after the first sync and before enabling mappings meets (1)–(3).
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect, a procedure for a different situation)**: Manually maintaining membership is the approach for JIT, which does not synchronize IdP group membership, and violates (3), which requires retaining SCIM.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Without group mappings, roles and seat types must be changed manually, violating (1), which requires automatic changes when group membership changes.

Additional note: Group mappings determine only role types and seat tiers. The organization's Primary Owner is excluded from group mappings and SCIM cleanup.

**Source documents**: [Set up JIT or SCIM provisioning (Claude) › Use custom roles with SCIM group mappings · Troubleshooting](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/13133195-set-up-jit-or-scim-provisioning)

questions.title: A licensed Gemini Enterprise user who cannot access certain features
questions.prompt: Hanbit Accounting uses Gemini Enterprise and authenticates employees through Microsoft Entra ID and Workforce Identity Federation. Some employees can sign in normally and have licenses assigned, but cannot use certain features. Other employees using the same integration can use those features without problems. The affected employees' licenses came from a different subscription type recently purchased, and nobody has verified whether they have the user role on the Gemini Enterprise project. Choose the two things to check first.

options.text: Check whether the subscription type associated with those licenses includes the features the employees want to use.
Check whether those employees have the Gemini Enterprise User role (`roles/discoveryengine.agentspaceUser`) on the Gemini Enterprise project.
Make the agent instructions more specific so the features execute.
Reset the employees' Entra ID passwords and have them sign in again.
Expand the sharing scope of the notebooks the employees created to the entire organization.

questions.explanation:
The relevant clues are "sign-in works," "licenses assigned," "a different subscription type," and "the role has never been checked." Having a license means the user can enter the system, but eligibility to use particular features (entitlement) is separately determined by the features included in the subscription type and IAM roles. Gemini Enterprise troubleshooting documentation advises checking whether the subscription type includes the feature, whether the Gemini Enterprise User role exists on the project, and whether Workforce Identity Federation is configured correctly when licensed users cannot access features. Here, other employees using the same integration work normally, making the first two checks more directly supported than the third.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: If the newly purchased subscription type does not include the feature, a license does not make that feature available.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: Without the project's user role, access can be blocked despite having a license.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect, confuses similar functions)**: Instructions determine how an agent responds, not eligibility to use features.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect, a procedure for a different situation)**: Sign-in already works, and other employees using the same integration have no problem, so this is not an authentication issue. Password resets address sign-in failures.
- **{{option:E}} (Incorrect, confuses similar functions)**: Notebook sharing determines who can view created content, not eligibility to use features.

Additional note: The documentation says a license is valid only in the project where it is assigned, so when purchasing another subscription, also verify that licenses were distributed to the correct project. The term "entitlement" does not appear in the document; it is used here generically for the feature scope included in a subscription type.

**Source documents**: [Frequently asked questions about Gemini Enterprise subscriptions and licenses › Why can't users access Gemini Enterprise features even though they have licenses?](https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini/enterprise/docs/licenses-faqs)

questions.title: Preserving Gemini Enterprise materials when employee email addresses change
questions.prompt:
Nuri Logistics uses Gemini Enterprise with Workforce Identity Federation and maps the user identifier `google.subject` to each employee's lowercase email address. Following a merger, every employee's email domain will change next month. A team lead uses several personal notebooks and one agent shared with 20 teammates. The requirements are:

- (1) Preserve the personal notebook and agent content the team lead wants to keep.
- (2) Allow the team lead to use Gemini Enterprise immediately after the email change.
- (3) Maintain continuity for the shared agent used by the 20 teammates.

What is the most appropriate action before the change?

options.text: Only change the email address in the IdP. Gemini Enterprise automatically migrates the previous identifier's conversation history, notebooks, and agents to the new identifier.
The licenses and IAM roles granted to the old identifier also apply to the new one, so change the email without other action and notify employees afterward.
Only preassign a license and roles to the new identifier, without separately notifying employees.

Notify employees before the change so they share personal notebooks and agents they want to retain; grant licenses and required roles to the new identifier, and transfer ownership of shared agents to the new identifier.

questions.explanation:
The relevant clues are the `google.subject` mapping and requirements (1)–(3). Gemini Enterprise documentation explains that `google.subject` is used for attribute mapping, license assignment, and notebook sharing. If the mapped value changes, it is treated as a new user: the old identifier's conversation history, notebooks, and agents become inaccessible, data is not migrated, and the previous licenses and IAM roles do not apply (identifier mapping). The documentation recommends three preparatory actions: notify employees and have them share personal agents and notebooks they want to retain; grant the new identifier licenses and required roles; and transfer ownership of agents shared with others to the new identifier.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect, factual error)**: The documentation explicitly states that data from the old identifier is not migrated to the new one.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect, factual error)**: The old identifier's licenses and IAM roles do not apply to the new one, blocking access immediately after the change and violating (2).
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect, violates a constraint)**: It meets (2), but employees cannot share personal materials beforehand, violating (1), and shared-agent ownership is not transferred, violating (3).
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: The three preparatory actions meet (1)–(3).

Additional note: Identifiers are case-sensitive, so even a change in capitalization creates a different identifier. New configurations are advised to map emails to lowercase.

**Source documents**: [Configure identity provider (Gemini Enterprise) › Attribute mapping · Before you change a user's identifier](https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini/enterprise/docs/configure-identity-provider)

questions.title: A ChatGPT app connected to a personal account cannot see team files
questions.prompt: An employee at Hanbit Accounting connects the Google Drive app in a ChatGPT Business workspace. Out of habit, they select their personal Google account. The app list shows "Connected," but work files in the team's shared drive cannot be found. All files the employee needs are accessible only through the work Google account. The team rule is that **work files must be accessed only using work-account permissions**. What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Connect the work account. If supported, add it using "Connect another account"; otherwise disconnect the personal account and reconnect using the work account.
Raise app permissions to "Allow all actions" so approval requests do not block searching.
Ask the workspace administrator to disable and reenable the Google Drive app.
Keep the personal account connected and paste the work-folder link into the instructions so the app reads the files at that link.

questions.explanation:
The relevant clues are "personal Google account" and "accessible only through the work account." OpenAI's help article advises selecting an account that already has access to the information needed when connecting an app, and explains that connecting a personal account does not grant access to files, channels, or records available only in a work account (account linking). Some apps support multiple accounts through "Connect another account," and disconnecting an account stops future access through it. In managed workspaces, administrators may need to enable the app or approve the account domain.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: Connecting the work account with the necessary access addresses the cause directly and follows the team rule.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect, confuses similar functions)**: App permissions only change when ChatGPT requests confirmation before using access it already has; they do not reveal files unavailable to the account.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect, a procedure for a different situation)**: This addresses an app blocked as "Disabled by admin." This app is connected and working; the cause is the account choice.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect, factual error)**: Providing a link does not allow reading a file if the connected account lacks permission to access it.

Additional note: Some apps use administrator-managed connections without individual sign-in, so employees do not choose an account for those apps. Disconnecting does not automatically delete existing conversations.

**Source documents**: [Connecting and managing app accounts (ChatGPT) › Connecting accounts to apps · Multiple accounts per app · Access and admin-managed connections](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/20001494-connecting-and-managing-app-accounts)

questions.title: Preventing the Microsoft 365 connector from reading files employees cannot access
questions.prompt:
Nuri Logistics' IT administrator wants to enable the Microsoft 365 connector in Claude Enterprise. The security team requires that the connector never read materials beyond the files an employee can already access. The requirements are:

- (1) Each employee must see only files they can already access.
- (2) Employees must be able to use it without individually going through a consent screen.
- (3) Do not grant permission for the app to read tenant files without a signed-in user.

What should the administrator do?

options.text: Consent to application permissions on behalf of the organization so the app can read necessary files without a signed-in user.
Because these are delegated permissions, have each employee consent and connect individually without administrator consent.
Have a Microsoft Entra Global Administrator consent to delegated permissions on behalf of the organization; employees then only authenticate with their own Microsoft accounts.
Consent only to read-only application permissions to limit the app to reading.

questions.explanation:
The relevant clues are requirements (1) and (3). Claude's help article explains that the Microsoft 365 connector uses delegated permissions and that Claude acts on behalf of each user, accessing only data the user can already see. It also requires a Microsoft Entra Global Administrator to approve the integration (admin consent) before anyone connects; after approval, members only authenticate without seeing a consent screen. Microsoft documentation distinguishes delegated permissions, in which an app cannot access anything the signed-in user cannot access, from application permissions (app roles), in which it can access all data associated with the permission without a signed-in user. Only administrators can consent to application permissions.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Application permissions can read tenant data without a user, making this an overprivileged configuration that violates (1) and (3).
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect, factual error)**: This connector requires Global Administrator approval before anyone connects, so leaving consent to individual employees is incorrect and also violates (2).
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: Delegated permissions satisfy (1) and (3), while a single administrator consent allows employees to proceed without a consent screen, satisfying (2).
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect, factual error)**: Even read-only application permissions access all data associated with the permission without a signed-in user. As Microsoft's example illustrates, a file-read application permission can read every file in the tenant.

Additional note: An Entra administrator can revoke individual permissions; calls requiring a revoked permission then fail with an error (see WFA-N9).

**Source documents**: [Set up the Microsoft 365 connector (Claude) › Admin consent · Delegated permissions](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/12542951-set-up-the-microsoft-365-connector) · [Overview of permissions and consent in the Microsoft identity platform (Microsoft Learn) › Delegated and application permissions](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity-platform/permissions-consent-overview)

questions.title: Requesting additional permissions only when needed
questions.prompt: An AI champion at Hanbit Accounting is designing the connection flow for an external "email organization tool" that uses Google accounts for sign-in. Its initial feature only reads Gmail; next quarter it will add "automatically schedule meetings" (writing to Google Calendar). The team rule is to **request only necessary permissions at the time they are needed, so users understand why they are required**. Which design best follows Google's authentication guidance?

options.text: Request Gmail, Calendar, and Drive permissions together on the first connection so no further consent is needed.
Once Gmail read access is granted, every future scope is automatically included, so make no separate request when scheduling launches.
Users cannot grant only some requested permissions, so deny access to the entire tool if they reject even one.
Request only the additional Calendar permission when the scheduling feature is first used; if the user declines, disable only that feature and let the rest remain usable.

questions.explanation:
The relevant clue is "only necessary permissions at the time they are needed." Google's OAuth guidance recommends incremental authorization: requesting user-data access "in context," at the point where the relevant feature needs it. This helps users understand why access is requested and adds new scopes while retaining previously granted ones. Users may grant only some of multiple requested permissions, so apps must check the scopes actually granted and handle missing permissions by disabling the features that need them.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Requesting permissions not yet needed violates the rule to request only necessary permissions when needed.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect, factual error)**: Consent applies only to the requested scopes. If a new scope is needed, it must be requested then.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect, factual error)**: Google's documentation says users can grant only some requested permissions and instructs apps to check the granted scopes and respond accordingly.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: It requests only the required scope at the relevant time and disables only the affected feature if denied, following the rule.

Additional note: Names and interfaces for requesting approval at the moment of need (JIT consent) differ by service. This question tests principles explained in Google's OAuth guidance; the interface behavior of ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini apps must be checked separately in each product's help documentation.

**Source documents**: [Using OAuth 2.0 for Web Server Applications (Google) › Incremental authorization · Granular permissions](https://developers.google.com/identity/protocols/oauth2/web-server)

questions.title: Matching disconnection, consent revocation, and administrator consent to actors and outcomes
questions.prompt: There are five situations in which administrators and members disconnect or approve external app connections. Match each situation on the left with the most appropriate action or outcome on the right. One right-hand option is unused.

options.text: The member disconnects their own connection under Customize > Connectors.
An organization Owner removes the connector for the entire organization.
Calls requiring that permission fail with a "Failed to call tool" error.
Future access through the disconnected account stops, but existing conversations are not automatically deleted.
A Microsoft Entra Global Administrator approves the integration (admin consent).
Each member consents on behalf of the organization on the consent screen.

items.text: A Claude Team member wants to disconnect only their own Microsoft 365 connector connection.
The Microsoft 365 connector must be removed from the entire Claude Team organization.
A Microsoft Entra administrator has revoked one individual permission granted to Claude.
A ChatGPT member has disconnected an app under Apps in Settings.
The organization wants to make Claude's Microsoft 365 connector available for the first time.

questions.explanation:
The matching criterion is who grants or withdraws consent, and at what scope. Individuals disconnect their own connections; an Owner removes the organization-wide connection; Microsoft-side administrators revoke individual permissions and provide initial approval. Revocation manifests as immediate call failures, while disconnection stops future access only.

| Number | Rationale |
| --- | --- |
| 1 → {{option:a}} | Claude's help article says members can disconnect their own integrations under Customize > Connectors. |
| 2 → {{option:b}} | The same help article says Owners on Team and Enterprise plans can remove the connector for the entire organization. |
| 3 → {{option:c}} | Entra administrators can revoke individual permissions; subsequent access to resources requiring that permission produces a "Failed to call tool" error. |
| 4 → {{option:d}} | OpenAI's help article explains that disconnecting stops future access through that account, but does not automatically delete existing conversations. |
| 5 → {{option:e}} | An Entra Global Administrator must approve the integration before anyone connects. After approval, members only authenticate without a consent screen. |
| {{option:f}} | Members cannot consent on behalf of the organization. Organization-wide approval is the administrator's responsibility, so this matches none of the situations and is unused. |

Additional note: ChatGPT's help article notes that the administrator at a provider such as Google or Microsoft may be a different person from the ChatGPT workspace administrator. After disconnecting, separately check permissions remaining in the provider-side account settings.

**Source documents**: [Set up the Microsoft 365 connector (Claude) › Revoking access · Admin consent](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/12542951-set-up-the-microsoft-365-connector) · [Connecting and managing app accounts (ChatGPT) › Disconnecting vs. deleting](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/20001494-connecting-and-managing-app-accounts)

questions.title: Connecting SharePoint access to Finance group membership
questions.prompt:
Connecting SharePoint access to Finance group membership

Which configuration meets [Requirement 1]?
questions.context:
[Company overview] Nuri Logistics is a logistics company using a ChatGPT Enterprise workspace. Its internal identity provider (IdP) is Okta, and SCIM synchronization is configured.

[Existing environment] About 25 finance employees belong to the IdP's "Finance" group. The workspace already has a custom role, "Finance document reader," that permits use of the SharePoint app. The Finance group is not currently linked to the workspace, and employees join through automatic account creation when signing in with company email addresses. Some members who joined through automatic account creation may not be SCIM-managed.

[Requirement 1] As new finance staff join or employees transfer departments, SharePoint app access must follow Finance group membership without an administrator changing settings for each person.

[Requirement 2] Departing finance employees must definitively lose workspace access, with a procedure to verify removal. Deleting their personal OpenAI accounts is not required.

[Note] One administrator suggested, "Simply give the Finance group the workspace owner role," and another suggested, "Only Finance uses the SharePoint app, so enable it for the entire workspace."

options.text: In the admin console's Product access section, assign the synchronized Finance group to the workspace to create the corresponding workspace group. Then have the workspace owner assign the "Finance document reader" role to that group under Permissions & roles > Role assignments.
When assigning the Finance group in the admin console's Product access editor, also specify the "Finance document reader" custom role there.
Assign the "Finance document reader" role through Direct roles in each finance employee's profile, and have an administrator revoke it when the employee changes departments.
Keep automatic account creation enabled, enable the SharePoint app for the entire workspace, and instruct employees outside Finance not to use it.

questions.explanation:
The relevant clues in [Requirement 1] are "without changing settings for each person" and "according to group membership." According to OpenAI's help article, assigning a synchronized group to a workspace creates a corresponding workspace group, and people who are not already members are invited with the Member role. The Product access editor does not assign workspace owner or custom workspace roles, so a workspace owner must assign the custom role under Permissions & roles within the workspace. The RBAC help article explains that roles can be assigned to SCIM-synchronized groups, recommends groups for management at scale, and states that role permissions are additive. Custom roles can control apps individually.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: It creates a workspace group from the synchronized group and attaches the role to it, so access changes with group membership.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect, factual error)**: The Product access editor does not assign custom workspace roles. These are assigned inside the workspace.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect, violates a constraint)**: The role is granted, but requires individual assignment and revocation on transfer, violating [Requirement 1].
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Automatic account creation is separate from SCIM and does not synchronize directory users and groups. Instructions are not access controls, so other employees can still use the app.

Additional note: The owner-role suggestion in [Note] is a distractor because that role cannot be assigned through Product access. Role permissions are additive, so if a transferring employee already has the same permission through another group or a direct role, leaving the old group may not remove access. Role changes can take up to five minutes to take effect.

**Source documents**: [SCIM provisioning and management (ChatGPT) › Product access · Groups](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/10011769-scim-provisioning-and-management) · [Managing feature access with role-based access control in ChatGPT › Custom roles · Role assignments](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/11750701-managing-feature-access-with-role-based-access-control-in-chatgpt)

questions.title: Verifying that a departed employee’s access has been removed
questions.prompt:
Verifying that a departed employee’s access has been removed

An Okta administrator "disabled" a departed finance employee but did not remove their ChatGPT app assignment. A workspace administrator removed the member in ChatGPT's admin console, yet the person reappeared as an active member a few days later. Which action meets [Requirement 2]?
questions.context:
[Company overview] Nuri Logistics is a logistics company using a ChatGPT Enterprise workspace. Its internal identity provider (IdP) is Okta, and SCIM synchronization is configured.

[Existing environment] About 25 finance employees belong to the IdP's "Finance" group. The workspace already has a custom role, "Finance document reader," that permits use of the SharePoint app. The Finance group is not currently linked to the workspace, and employees join through automatic account creation when signing in with company email addresses. Some members who joined through automatic account creation may not be SCIM-managed.

[Requirement 1] As new finance staff join or employees transfer departments, SharePoint app access must follow Finance group membership without an administrator changing settings for each person.

[Requirement 2] Departing finance employees must definitively lose workspace access, with a procedure to verify removal. Deleting their personal OpenAI accounts is not required.

[Note] One administrator suggested, "Simply give the Finance group the workspace owner role," and another suggested, "Only Finance uses the SharePoint app, so enable it for the entire workspace."

options.text: Remove the member again in ChatGPT's admin console and check daily whether they reappear.

Remove the user's ChatGPT app assignment in Okta. After the next successful sync, verify that they are no longer an active member, check for access remaining through direct invitations, other groups, or product-specific roles, and review seat assignments.
Treat the process as complete without further verification because SCIM deprovisioning deletes the OpenAI account.
Enable automatic account creation to synchronize the IdP user status with workspace membership status.

questions.explanation:
The relevant clues are "disabled but the app assignment was not removed" and "reappeared a few days later." OpenAI's help article explains that disabling a user in the IdP does not always remove the app assignment, and removing a member only in ChatGPT may be temporary if the IdP continues assigning them. After deprovisioning, it advises verifying after the next successful sync that group-derived access is gone, checking paths that may preserve separate access—such as direct invitations, other groups, and product-specific roles—confirming the person is no longer active, and reviewing seat assignments.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect, a procedure for a different situation)**: Removal only in ChatGPT is temporary if the IdP continues assigning the user. Repeated removal is a workaround that leaves the underlying IdP assignment in place.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: It removes the causal IdP assignment and checks membership status, remaining access paths, and seats after synchronization, providing the verification procedure required by [Requirement 2].
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect, factual error)**: Deprovisioning removes workspace membership, not the OpenAI account or personal workspace, and the documentation also prescribes verification.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect, confuses similar functions)**: Automatic account creation is separate from SCIM and does not synchronize directory users and groups. The documentation advises turning it off when planning to manage users through SCIM.

Additional note: Users who joined through automatic account creation may not be SCIM-managed, so removing them in the IdP may leave access intact. If the two methods are mixed as in this case, standardizing on SCIM management is safer. Contact OpenAI support if problems persist.

**Source documents**: [SCIM provisioning and management (ChatGPT) › Deprovisioning · Automatic account creation](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/10011769-scim-provisioning-and-management)

guide:
### 1. Introduction

**Purpose**: This exam assesses whether candidates can automate repetitive team work without coding by combining custom assistants, knowledge spaces, connectors, and agent features.

**Objectives**

- Translate business requirements into assistant instructions, knowledge files, and connector configurations.
- Choose static knowledge uploads or live connectors as appropriate.
- Place human confirmation checkpoints before irreversible actions.
- Minimize permissions and data exposure when sharing with teams.
- Evaluate and improve assistant quality with test-question sets.

### 2. Target candidates

- Workflow automation specialists, operations specialists, no-code developers, business analysts

**Recommended background and exam scope**

- ALF-level knowledge and at least six months of experience using generative AI at work are recommended. API coding is out of scope.

### 3. Content domains

| Domain | Weight |
| --- | --- |
| 1. Instruction and prompt design | 25% |
| 2. Knowledge-based assistant configuration | 25% |
| 3. Connector and agent workflows | 25% |
| 4. Sharing, permissions, and data management | 15% |
| 5. Quality verification and improvement | 10% |

**Domain 1: Instruction and prompt design**

- Knowledge: System-level versus conversational instructions; incorporating examples, output formats, and prohibitions; prioritizing lengthy instructions.
- Skills: Turn team manuals into instructions producing consistent results; fix behavior caused by conflicting instructions.

**Domain 2: Knowledge-based assistant configuration**

- Knowledge: How files uploaded to projects, GPTs, and Gems (scheduled for retirement or in transition) are used; limitations by file format and volume; frequently changing versus fixed material.
- Skills: Choose uploads or connectors to minimize operational burden based on update frequency and volume.

**Domain 3: Connector and agent workflows**

- Knowledge: Connector principles, including remote MCP servers; read versus write access; workspace-agent operation.
- Skills: Place confirmation before hard-to-reverse actions such as sending email or editing documents; select minimum necessary connector permissions.

**Domain 4: Sharing, permissions, and data management**

- Knowledge: Team and organization sharing scopes, administrator-controlled features, enterprise-plan retention policies.
- Skills: Share assistants containing sensitive material only with necessary people.

**Domain 5: Quality verification and improvement**

- Knowledge: Representative question sets, correct-answer criteria, failure types including omissions, fabrications, and formatting errors.
- Skills: Determine whether failures require instruction, knowledge, or connector changes.
